title: Bills news: Brandon Beane feels ‘really good’ about roster
summary: Before Tuesday’s practice session, Bills general manager Brandon Beane met with the media to reflect on Buffalo’s roster going into the 2026 regular season and the decisions that informed who made the 53-man roster. Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by recapping what Beane and head coach Joe Brady had to say about the […]
full_text: Brandon Beane, general manager of then Buffalo Bills, heads off the field at the end of practice at the Buffalo Bills training camp at St. John Fisher University in Pittsford on July 24, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Before Tuesday’s practice session, Bills general manager Brandon Beane met with the media to reflect on Buffalo’s roster going into the 2026 regular season and the decisions that informed who made the 53-man roster. Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by recapping what Beane and head coach Joe Brady had to say about the roster, including why Beane feels “really good about what’s on the 53,” and why Brady is excited to see what Buffalo’s “unique tight end room” can do this year. Check out the assessments below and then let us know your thoughts on whether Buffalo’s roster is better than last year. How the Bills constructed their 53-man roster During his session with reporters, Brandon Beane addressed how he went about constructing Buffalo’s 53-man roster, along with several bigger-picture questions facing the team. When the roster cuts were made, some fans were surprised that Beane opted for three true boundary cornerbacks in Christian Benford, Maxwell Hairston and Davison Igbinosun, though it should be noted Jordan Hancock can also be deployed here. For as much as Beane said the Bills needed to add more talent to their cornerback room this offseason, Beane said he’s happy with the cornerbacks heading into the season. And when it comes to who starts opposite Benford, Brady has already named Hairston as CB2 while Beane expressed confidence in Hairston’s abilities. “We have a lot of confidence in (Hairston),” Beane said. “I think IGB has done a really good job. If we didn’t have confidence in him, we’d just sit him down and throw IGB in. He’s a young player that’s gonna continue to push his way, and Max knows that he’ll have to play at a certain level, or there’s a young man here that’s ready to showcase kind of what he can do.” Another surprise move was Buffalo’s decision to keep four tight ends—Dalton Kincaid, Dawson Knox, Jackson Hawes and Keleki Latu—on the active roster. Brady said the team is looking forward to utilizing “such a unique tight end room that you have the ability to build a lot of different structures and play 10 personnel sets, 20 personnel sets and do a lot of different things with that. title: Plays That Defined 2025: Bills at Broncos, Divisional Round
summary: The 2025 Buffalo Bills season has been written, but the book is incomplete. Before we cast our full attention toward the 2026 season, let’s take one last glance back over our shoulder for our annual look at the Plays That Defined the prior campaign. For any newcomers, first and foremost; Welcome! When it comes to […]
full_text: DENVER , CO - JANUARY 17: Ja'quan McMillian (29) of the Denver Broncos rips an interception from Brandin Cooks (18) of the Buffalo Bills during overtime of the Broncos' 33-30 win at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colorado on Saturday, January 17, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images The 2025 Buffalo Bills season has been written, but the book is incomplete. Before we cast our full attention toward the 2026 season, let’s take one last glance back over our shoulder for our annual look at the Plays That Defined the prior campaign. For any newcomers, first and foremost; Welcome! When it comes to the “rules” of this exercise, we’re not voting for our favorite highlight necessarily, but the one that best captures the essence of the game. Put differently, if you had to choose just one play to show someone to explain as much of the contest as possible, which would you choose? Divisional Round: Buffalo Bills at Denver Broncos The Bills had survived a thriller in Jacksonville to earn the right to move on to the Divisional Round. Up next was the Denver Broncos and I’ll be candid right away for this entry into the series. With all due respect to the Broncos and their fans, no one watching this game should come away with the impression that the better team won. Buffalo turned the ball over five times. FIVE! One wasn’t really but it still counted as one. One turnover was a play that will likely haunt Josh Allen for eternity. Of Denver’s seven scoring drives, four of them came off of turnovers. The one that the Bills forced on defense was immediately negated by the offense turning the ball over. Again. Yes, the officiating left a lot to be desired. There’s no way to get around it though, Buffalo had every opportunity to put this game away and squandered like few teams have ever squandered. There will be no highlights to choose from for this game, only despair. AAAAGGGGGGHHH! (Q1; 8:30) Plays That Defined 2025 – Divisional Round – AAAAAAAHHHHHHGGGG pic.twitter.com/klPmyjKOEi — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 15, 2026 With all the other bull**** from this game, I bet you forgot about this, didn’t you? Well yours truly, aka “The ***hole who spends way too much time on penalties” didn’t forget. This was on the Broncos’ first drive where they put up a field goal. Three-point swing from that little bit of Larry Ogunjobi’s hand going over the line pre-snap. Can anyone tell me again how close the final result was? Whatever the **** you want to call this (Q2; 0:16) Plays That Defined 2025 – Divisional Round – What the **** was this? pic.twitter.com/SkETps3IcH — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 15, 2026 Let’s jump into the NFL Quarterback simulator (possibly assisted by Trent Edwards*). You have the ball. There’s 16 seconds left in the first half. You’re down by seven. The head coach wants to try one play and hope for a miracle. As you scramble due to the play being busted, you have a choice. Do you end the play and gracefully go into the half knowing you’re only down one score? Or do you recklessly and DELIBERATELY put the ball on the ground knowing the opponent will already be in field goal range if they recover? Easy choice right? I still love you Josh Allen, but once again remind me how close of a game this turned out to be? *Did you remember that Trent Edwards was co-founder of a virtual reality quarterback deal? This is the kind of thing occupying my brain rather than useful knowledge. The “Interception” (OT; 7:55) Plays That Defined 2025 – Divisional Round – The Interception pic.twitter.com/dbO5kNtUVB — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 15, 2026 This is a catch in field goal range and while I know I’m supposed to be impartial I’m pretty confident this is going to win the whole darn thing this year and I’m not saying it’s the wrong choice but please at least pay attention to the other selections I’ve put out there this year because it was a lot of work and this is a run-on sentence and that’s fine because we all know how this is going to end, don’t we? Pass interference (OT; 6:09) Plays That Defined 2025 – Divisional Round – Pass interference pic.twitter.com/UqcX6LqSC2 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 15, 2026 Read my full penalty analysis here , where I also dive into the officiating a bit. The short version is that I don’t love the pass interference on Taron Johnson here and think it should have been offsetting if anything was called. There’s also the matter of Joey Bosa deciding to impact the game by getting a roughing the passer call on the same play so it’s all a convoluted mess. In the end, since they did call the defensive pass interference, yours truly feels they should have called the similar contact by the receiver and put the ball back where it was. That gives the Bills another crack at stopping this drive and we all know I prefer a shot to stop them vs. “flag putting them right in field goal range.” You stopped reading this article when you saw the last play didn’t you? Did you read any of this? You didn’t, did you? I bet you just scrolled down to the poll knowing that “interception” was on the list. Who am I even addressing here? None of you got this far. Maybe Matt B. or Chris felt obligated to read this far and edit to make sure I didn’t go off the rails. Nah. I bet even they tuned out. Anyway, go Bills! Time to start writing some content that isn’t overshadowed by such a downer of a play. Which play best defines the Bills’ crushing defeat?

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 10 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE , NC - NOVEMBER 16: Dan Morgan #55 of the Carolina Panthers participates in warm-ups before a game against the Washington Redskins on November 16, 2003 at Ericsson Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Sporting News via Getty Images via Getty Images) | Sporting News via Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #10. Dan Morgan There aren’t many people in NFL history who had successful careers on the field and turned that into notable, successful careers in NFL front offices, especially for the team they played for. Dan Morgan is already in rarified air from an NFL history perspective, but his skill on the field and as GM (so far) have both been above average. Morgan ended his collegiate career at The U with a dominant senior year. The awards flooded in for that 2000 season: Big East Defensive Player of the Year, Bronko Nagurski Award, Chuck Bednarik Award, Dick Butkus Award, and unanimous First Team All-American. The following 2001 NFL Draft, the Panthers used the 11th overall pick to take Morgan, immediately bolstering their defense. Despite his ability on the field, his body could not handle the NFL game on a regular basis. Morgan started 11 games at strong side linebacker his rookie year, making the All-Rookie Team. That season could have been even more exceptional, but Morgan broke his leg late in the season and was put on IR. He returned the following year and took over the middle of the defense. Groin and shoulder injuries limited Morgan to just eight games his sophomore season, but he was dynamic in the games he played. He was able to recover a bit in the 2003 season as he helped captain the dominant Panthers defense on their first Super Bowl run in franchise history. A pulled hammy and his first career concussion limited him to just 11 regular season games, but he was healthy and dominant in the postseason, including a still Super Bowl record 18 tackles against the Patriots. His health stayed solid in 2004 as well, allowing him to play in 12 games and earn his first and only Pro Bowl selection. He tallied 102 tackles, two sacks, two interceptions, a forced fumble, two fumble recoveries, and six passes defended. In 2005, he played a career-high 13 games and was a force on the field, though his counting stats took a dip. Unfortunately, the 2006 season was the beginning of the end physically for Dan Morgan. He missed the final 15 games after suffering two severe concussions within a month. He came back for the 2007 season with specialized padding and a protective mouthpiece, which seemed to be working. Concussions weren’t the death knell, though, it was an Achilles tear in Week 3 that did him in. He tried to make a comeback with the New Orleans Saints in both 2008 and 2009, but his physical health denied him the opportunity to see the field. He immediately transitioned to the front office side of the NFL, joining the Seahawks as a scouting intern in 2010. He was promoted to Assistant Director of Pro Personnel in 2011, then became the Seahawks Director of Pro Personnel in 2015 after helping the team win the Super Bowl. In 2018, Morgan moved to the Buffalo Bills and was given the Director of Player Personnel position directly under General Manager (and former Panthers front office member) Brandon Beane. Morgan returned to Carolina in 2021 as the Assistant General Manager under Scott Fitterer. After Fitterer was relieved of his duties in 2024, Morgan took the interim job and made enough of an impression that he was hired as the full time replacement. He has been the Panthers General Manager since then, playing a major role in the upward trajectory the last couple of seasons including hiring Dave Canales, drafting some young and promising players, filling major holes in free agency, and making shrewd trades for veteran contributors. While he has definitely taken his lumps and learned on the fly, he seems to be steering the ship in the right direction. While his playing career was shortened by injuries, his dominance while on the field and his decisions so far as GM land him in the top ten on our list.

While most folks discount preseason records as largely meaningless, most folks are also already crowning the Rams as […]
full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 06: Head coach Dave Canales of the Carolina Panthers looks on during the first quarter of the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Game against the Arizona Cardinals at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 06, 2026 in Canton, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images With the benefit of an extra game thanks to the Hall of Fame game, the Carolina Panthers had the second best record in the NFC at 3-1. They were second only to the 3-0 Los Angeles Rams. While most folks discount preseason records as largely meaningless, most folks are also already crowning the Rams as Super Bowl Champions. I see no reason why we can’t go ahead and pencil the Panthers in as the #2 seed in the NFC for the 2026 playoffs. Right? All joking aside, this was the strongest performance the Panthers have had in a preseason since their ill-fated 2018 season. That shows how much the roster has recently recovered after years of mismanagement by former head coach and general manager combos. The Carolina Panthers may actually employ NFL-level talent. Huzzah. That’s all well and good, but it doesn’t necessarily change the fact that the Panthers have been notorious for slow starts to their seasons under the leadership of head coach Dave Canales and quarterback Bryce Young. Who is responsible and why that has happened at all is a complicated question without a simple answer. A deep roster, while hugely important, does not mean that the starters are going to be ready for Week 1. The limited action we saw from those starters in this preseason did not inspire a lot of confidence that 2026 was going to be a brand new year for the Panthers. A mixed bag is about par for the course for us. Which brings us to this week’s Reacts survey question. title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 11 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: Carolina Panthers defensive tackle Kris Jenkins (77) smiles as he heads to the team's bench following his sack of Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Ben Roethlisberger in the first quarter of NFL preseason football at the Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina, Thursday, August 30, 2007. (Photo by Jeff Siner/Charlotte Observer/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #11. Kris Jenkins We’re in the middle of the golden age of Carolina Panthers history in this countdown right now. The list is rife with players from the early to mid 2000s when the Panthers had a feared defense and were one of the least desirable teams to play in the NFL. We continue that trend with today’s topic of the countdown, the anchor of that defense, Kris Jenkins. The Panthers selected Jenkins in the second round of the 2001 NFL Draft while the team was in a hot streak of adding elite talent. He quickly solidified himself as a starter as a rookie, and built upon that in the subsequent seasons. In his second year, Jenkins racked up seven sacks and 15 tackles for a loss, earning Pro Bowl and All Pro honors. He followed that up with an almost identical season en route to his second Pro Bowl and All Pro nominations. He had two seasons derailed by injuries but was able to come back and contribute two more solid seasons in Carolina before he was traded to the Jets. He had one last dominant season in New York before ACL tears ended each of the next two years, and ultimately his career. Jenkins clocked in at 6’5”, 320 pounds at the combine, but he was often listed closer to 350 pounds during his career. He was a behemoth of a man that was practically immovable at the line of scrimmage. His sheer size allowed him to clog up space, and his length and strength further extended the range of his impact. He was able to generate decent pressure by nose tackle standards purely with his strength and ability to push the line. He used those physical attributes and motor to also pull off one of the most impressive special teams feats in league history. He blocked two field goals in one game against the Buccaneers. One of them was an extra point that would’ve won the game for Tampa. Instead, the Panthers ended up winning the game in overtime. Jenkins’ career probably didn’t reach the heights it could have due to injury. He tore his ACL three times during his time in the NFL, and the last two ultimately ended his career. His peak years were about as dominant as they come for an interior defensive lineman, and he was an essential part of the Panthers’ Super Bowl run in 2003. For that, he lands at number 11 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: Which Chicago Bears Practice Squad Player Will Make the Biggest Impact?
summary: With roster cuts in the rearview and practice squads across the league all but finalized for opening day, we ask the following question: Which current practice squad player will make the biggest impact? You can take a look at Chicago’s practice squad in depth here, but for me, this answer boils down to three players. […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - AUGUST 22: Chicago Bears wide receiver Kaden Davis (27) carries the ball during the preseason game between the Chicago Bears and the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images With roster cuts in the rearview and practice squads across the league all but finalized for opening day, we ask the following question: Which current practice squad player will make the biggest impact? You can take a look at Chicago’s practice squad in depth here , but for me, this answer boils down to three players. Salvon Ahmed – Running Back Ahmed was having a strong camp and explosive preseason before finally being cut and landing on the PS. Averaging 6 yards per carry and taking a screen pass 49 yards for a TD highlighted his training camp experience, but Ahmed routinely made plays in camp and looked every bit deserving of a roster spot. Kaden Davis – Wide Receiver Kaden Davis was my surprise of camp. Undrafted in the 2022 NFL Draft, Davis, AKA “White Lightning,” never recorded a single catch in the regular season and only returned four kickoffs – all with the Browns, according to Pro Football Reference. After spending time with the Lions practice squad, Davis showed up in Chicago and made more plays than arguably anyone else. I was actually expecting him to make the final 53, but not surprised to see him at least land on the PS. Marcus Davenport – DE Drafted in the first round of the 2018 NFL Draft by the New Orleans Saints, Davenport joined Dennis Allen’s defense and notched 4.5 sacks as a rookie. Standing 6’6” and weighing 265lb (though I am guessing it’s much closer to 300 these days), Davenport is a prototypical Dennis Allen 4-3 DE. How much he has left in the tank, however, is another question. Especially after struggling through injuries his entire career and only once starting more than 9 games in a season. Added to a thin DE rotation, Davenport could be leaned upon heavily. My pick? Salvon Ahmed . The running back brought a burst that only starter D’Andre Swift possesses in both the run and pass game and comes in knowing new RB coach Eric Studesville’s run scheme, as he formerly played for Studesville in Miami. Weather it’s in the return game or spelling Swift and Monangai on offense, I expect Ahmed to have more of an impact than any other practice squad player in 2026. What about you? Which Practice Squad player do you feel makes the greatest impact this season?

title: Chicago Bears have the worst net penalty yards over the last 4 years
summary: Fans, rejoice. Real data backs up the shouting at televisions, cussing in cars, booing at Soldier Field and angry posts on social media for years. The refs really do have it out for the Chicago Bears. Football savant and data analytics master Warren Sharp of Sharp Football Analysis dove deep into the penalty yards against […]
full_text: Matt Lafleur plotting with the refs against Chicago, probably. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) Fans, rejoice. Real data backs up the shouting at televisions, cussing in cars, booing at Soldier Field and angry posts on social media for years. The refs really do have it out for the Chicago Bears . Football savant and data analytics master Warren Sharp of Sharp Football Analysis dove deep into the penalty yards against Chicago and against their opponents, and the results held true to what’s been known online as the “Bears tax.” The Bears are at the bottom of the penalty yardage discrepancy. Both in terms of yards against them and yards called against their opponents. From the article: Over the last four years, having very few penalties called on their opponents has been the standard for Chicago. Bears opponent’s rank penalty yards: 2025: #1 fewest 2024: #7 fewest 2023: #1 fewest 2022: #1 fewest And over the last four years combined: Bears rank in penalty yards called against opponents? #1 fewest Bears rank in penalties called against opponents? #1 fewest But it’s not just infrequent penalties called against opponents. There’s also this: First downs awarded TO THE BEARS via penalties called on opponents? #1 fewest Which means Chicago’s net penalty yards (yards awarded to the Bears by penalty and those against) since 2022 is the highest in the league by over 200 yards. net penalty yards since 2022: -795 – Chicago Bears <<huge gap>> -584 – New York Jets -507 – Tennessee Titans -454 – New England Patriots -416 – Baltimore Ravens -356 – Denver Broncos -307 – Kansas City Chiefs -276 – Arizona Cardinals -268 – Houston Texans -234 – Philadelphia… — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) May 8, 2026 It goes even further. Many fans have pointed out over the years the beatings taken by former quarterback Justin Fields and, more recently, by Caleb Williams, so it comes as no surprise the Bears have earned the fewest roughing the passer calls by opponents. But Chicago’s defense has been called for the most. A total of 7 called on the Bears’ opponents and 17 on Chicago’s defense. Bears opponents also had the fewest DPI penalties, the third-fewest unnecessary roughness calls when facing Chicago and the fourth-fewest holding penalties (looking at you Green Bay!). The whole article is fascinating and worth a look. Do Bears fans have a real gripe? The numbers say they do.

title: Report: Chicago Bears Exploring Trade Market for Defensive Ends
summary: A discussion pertaining to the Chicago Bears’ defensive line and their need for improvement is about as predictable and common as seeing a proper Chicago-style dog featuring an all-beef frank on a poppy-seed bun. For the most part, defensive end has been largely untouched, aside from their recent signing of Marcus Davenport. That might very […]
full_text: TEMPE, ARIZONA - JUNE 09: Josh Sweat #10 of the Arizona Cardinals looks on during a mandatory minicamp at Dignity Health Arizona Cardinals Training Center on June 09, 2026 in Tempe, Arizona. (Photo by Chris Coduto/Getty Images) | Getty Images A discussion pertaining to the Chicago Bears’ defensive line and their need for improvement is about as predictable and common as seeing a proper Chicago-style dog featuring an all-beef frank on a poppy-seed bun. For the most part, defensive end has been largely untouched, aside from their recent signing of Marcus Davenport. That might very well be changing in the near future. Per Dan Graziano of ESPN the Chicago Bears are reportedly (still) involved with the trade market for a new defensive end . By the phrasing of his article, it sounds like an actual starter adjacent from Montez Sweat. Someone who could command a sizeable return in any deal. Don’t be surprised if … the Bears still trade for an edge rusher. What I’m hearing: Chicago is thin on defense, especially on the back end. But it’s up front where the team is still looking for a strong edge presence opposite Montez Sweat . The Bears added veteran Marcus Davenport a couple of weeks ago, but that move doesn’t appear to be working out; they let Davenport go in their initial cut down to 53 players over the weekend before bringing him back on the practice squad. Bears GM Ryan Poles has been an active and aggressive trader in his time with the team, and he’ll turn over every rock he can looking for an impact player up front. The Bears’ health issues on defense might be more concentrated on the back end, but improving the pass rush would help the secondary, too. This, of course, is not the first time the Bears have been tied into trade rumors for bolstering their group of down linemen on defense. Earlier in the spring came confirmation by general manager Ryan Poles himself on their interest in Maxx Crosby. There was also a documented interest in Vita Vea shortly before his contract extension was finalized. And there has been a precedent set in Chicago for late major trades involving DL dating back to 2004. August 21st 2004: Jerry Angelo trades for Adewale Ogunleye August 31st 2018: Ryan Pace trades for Khalil Mack October 31st 2023: Ryan Poles trades for Montez Sweat Even at the trade deadline last year — and to a much lesser extent — the Bears acquired Joe Tyron-Shoyinka from the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. This, along with Ryan Poles’ overall history of swinging big trades, has everyone curious as to what his next move will be. For a team pursuing their first Super Bowl Championship in decades, you’d have to imagine everything (reasonable) is on the table. Coming off the heels of their latest trade shipping Gervon Dexter Sr to the Atlanta Falcons, the Bears seem poised to make their next appearance at bat for the market. Who they’re targeting — Maxx Crosby, Josh Sweat, etc. — is unknown. And whether this is a Pete Crow-Armstrong, AKA MVPete-sized swing, remains to be seen as well.

full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - AUGUST 29: Qadir Ismail #80 of the Chicago Bears after the preseason game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears have begun signing players to their initial 2026 practice squad, but the list will be fluid, and we’ll update it throughout the year. Here are the first 11 signed players per the NFL transaction wire, but a couple of others were reported earlier today and are listed in our tracker . There will be other players added to the practice squad tomorrow. UPDATE (9/2): The Bears have signed tight end Qadir Ismail. UPDATE (9/1): The Bears have also signed RB Zavier Scott, LB Buddy Johnson, and OL Christian Jones. Caden Barnett, OG Kyle Hergel, iOL Christian Jones, OT Salvon Ahmed, RB Zavier Scott, RB Scotty Miller, WR Kaden Davis, WR J.P Richardson, WR Stephen Carlson, TE Qadir Ismail, TE Wayne Matthews III, LB Buddy Johnson, LB Marlen Sewell, S Deantre Prince, CB Marcus Davenport, DE Here are the qualifications for practice squad eligibility and some rules to remember. A 17th player is permitted as long as he qualifies for the NFL’s International Pathway Program. Players with no accrued seasons (rookies) and those with fewer than nine regular-season games in their lone accrued season. A maximum of ten players are allowed who have earned no more than two accrued seasons. Up to six players with unlimited accrued seasons are permitted on the practice squad. However, the number of players in the last two categories cannot exceed 10 total players. Teams can elevate up to two practice squad players for each game, but they can still only have 48 players active on game day. After the game, the elevated player(s) will revert to the practice squad. A player can be elevated up to three times, but if he’s needed after that, the team would be required to sign him to the 53-man active roster. Players on practice squads are free agents who can be signed to another team’s active roster. A player’s current club can’t block him from leaving; they can only make a counteroffer to keep him. Ultimately, it’s the player’s decision. If a player is signed away, his new team must keep him on its 53-man roster for three weeks, but if he’s released, he’ll revert to his previous team. Players signed to another active roster are also guaranteed three weeks’ salary. A practice squad player can’t sign with his team’s upcoming opponent unless he does so six days before the upcoming game or ten days prior if his team is on its bye week.

title: One Chicago Bears Fan’s Open Letter to Kyler Gordon
summary: Kyler, You are a Chicago Bear. As a 51-year-old former high-school football player who dreamed of one day following in the footsteps of Butkus and Singletary, let me tell you, you have been given one of the rarest opportunities in the world: stepping onto the NFL gridiron as a Chicago Bear. Bears greats are revered for […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 10: Kyler Gordon #6 of the Chicago Bears reacts as he takes the field prior to an NFL wild card playoff game against the Green Bay Packers at Soldier Field on January 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kyler, You are a Chicago Bear. As a 51-year-old former high-school football player who dreamed of one day following in the footsteps of Butkus and Singletary, let me tell you, you have been given one of the rarest opportunities in the world: stepping onto the NFL gridiron as a Chicago Bear. Bears greats are revered for their lifetimes. They are talked about – decades after their playing careers have ended. And in your career up to last year, while you’ve had your share of injuries, you were on a trajectory of being, if not one of the greats, at least in the Hall of Very Good. And we love our very good Chicago Bears. We cherish them. Especially if you play on the defensive side of the ball. You were a second-round pick of Ryan Poles in his first draft. You have been regarded as one of the better starting nickelbacks in the NFL, in an NFL game that increasingly relies on the nickelback position. You even have a cool superhero name, Spider-Man, to go along with the Bears’ Marvel theme with Iceman and the Hulk. But hey, when Hulk decided he didn’t want to play football anymore – he retired. You were given a three-year, $40 million extension. The job tens of thousands of athletes who have worked and sweated and gritted through the pain that is an everyday part of playing football would trade almost anything to have for just one Sunday – it is yours. How amazing is that? You only have to choose to step on the field, and you will get to bask in the adulation of thousands of Bears fans – playing a kids’ game, a game that is setting you and your family up for life. So, my guy – exactly what is the deal here? Last year you played three regular-season games and two in the playoffs. A lost season – but you came back at the end, and you contributed. This year the calf (or whatever the latest “soft tissue” injury that you’re dealing with is) has kept you off the field through OTAs, minicamp, and all of training camp. The team moved you to reserve/PUP. You will miss at least the first four games – and there are rumblings you may have played your last game for the Bears – despite being under contract until 2028. Your general manager, Ryan Poles, stood at a podium and admitted, despite the fact he remains “hopeful,” that he does not know if you will play for the Bears again. That is not media noise. It is not fans jumping the gun. That is the organization telling the city it is tired of waiting. And I won’t even mention the vibes coming from Ben Johnson when he is asked about you. It is…well…it is not good. Soft-tissue injuries hurt – sure. Calf strains can linger. Rehab is miserable – my guy, I know, having rehabbed an ACL and a biceps tear. Nobody is asking you to pretend otherwise. What people are asking is: why? Why has this one stretched from last August through another entire offseason and into September while the rest of the roster is preparing to play football? While Ozzy Trapillo has, by some miraculous feat of recovery, come back to practice after suffering a patella tendon tear in the playoffs. Look, here is the deal. Plenty of players in this league push through discomfort, manage the same kinds of issues that it is reported that you have been dealing with, and they get on the field. Hell, I don’t mean to go all, old man, up-the-hill-both-ways-in-the-snow on you, but Ronnie Lott once cut a finger off rather than get reconstructive surgery in order to keep playing. And look, we don’t have to go back to the 80s here. Your teammates – like Ozzy – are doing it. The guys who will take your snaps in Weeks 1–4 are doing it. And, Kyler, what a time to be a Chicago Bear! We won the division last year. We won a playoff game against the Packers. We were one play away from making the NFL championship game. Don’t you want to be part of that? I can’t speak for you, buddy, but I would give my left…well…a precious thing…to have the opportunity to suit up for the Bears and contribute to their first Super Bowl run since 2006 and their first Super Bowl win since 1985. You have that chance! It is right in front of you. You are a young man, and now you have a premium contract that has rewarded you for your play, but at the same time sets an expectation that you will give your all to live up to that contract and play your heart out for the Chicago Bears. And it won’t be your last if you do. But you play at a position that rewards availability as much as talent. We know you have the talent. Your availability is clearly in question. They say the best ability is availability. If you want to have a great NFL career and earn, not just this contract, but the next one, you need to be available. But the window is not infinite. Every week you sit is a week someone else learns the defense, earns trust, and makes the case that the slot can function without you. Heck, Kyler, the Bears just traded Dexter for a guy who is clearly intended to replace you. Ryan Poles and Ben Johnson have already said the quiet part out loud: you are not in their plans for the season – if you are in their plans at all. I cannot for the life of me understand why you seem to be fine with this happening. Look, football is a dangerous sport. And it is nowhere more dangerous than in the NFL. But that is the game you have spent your life practicing and preparing to play. And you have such a short window within which to play it. What I want to hear from you is that you can’t wait to get back on that field and you are doing everything possible to make that happen. That you take the contract you signed seriously and have every intention and desire to fulfill it. But you were talking about fashion and clothes in a fan interview recently… doesn’t exactly say “football is my #1 priority,” does it? Well, here we are. The season is just days away. You are going to miss the first four games of it, no doubt. And if you are dealing with some mysterious but truly debilitating injury that is keeping you from playing – hey – you have my sympathy and my apologies for questioning you. But you have to admit – those questions are understandable and reasonable. You are working on the record for “length of recovery from a soft tissue injury” and, my friend, that is not a record you want to set. Kyler, the schedule does not wait. Soldier Field, and the players who step onto it, and the fans who will cheer for those men – will not wait. Will it be you who is lining up against Kraft, or Hendrickson, or LaPorta this season? Will it be you blitzing from the nickel slot, just as Dennis Allen envisioned you would when he joined the team as our defensive coordinator? Will it be you picking off Jordan Love when he throws against his body late in a play back across the field? Or will it be someone else? Come back. Get back out there. Be the Spider-Man we all know you can be. Help lead us into the playoffs and beyond. Please. Sincerely, A Bears fan who wants nothing more than to see you do a backflip and shoot invisible webs at a Chicago Bears game in the VERY near future. D GOOCH
author: Donald Gooch

title: Question of the Day: After Jaylon Johnson, who do you trust in the secondary?
summary: After the draft in April, Bears fans were pretty excited, and for good reason, about the new-look secondary. After signing Coby Bryant and drafting Dillon Thieneman, Bears fans were excited about the new safety tandem with a healthy Jaylon Johnson and Kyler Gordon, and to be fair, a question mark with Tyrique Stevenson. But two […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Jaylon Johnson #1 of the Chicago Bears gets set during the second quarter of an NFL divisional playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images After the draft in April, Bears fans were pretty excited, and for good reason, about the new-look secondary. After signing Coby Bryant and drafting Dillon Thieneman, Bears fans were excited about the new safety tandem with a healthy Jaylon Johnson and Kyler Gordon, and to be fair, a question mark with Tyrique Stevenson. But two significant dents have hit the secondary. Coby Bryant is going to be out, at minimum, for a significant part of the season following an injury. Kyler Gordon hasn’t played, and now there are questions about whether he will even end up playing a down this season in Chicago. The depth in the secondary wasn’t great heading into camp, and with those two developments, suddenly, the Bears’ secondary went from a strength to a pretty big question mark. So that leaves us this question: After Jaylon Johnson, who do you trust most in the secondary? The biggest positive development for the Bears secondary has been the play of Jaylon Johnson in training camp. He’s looked like his old self, and if he provides lockdown coverage for Chicago, it will be a huge boost for the team. But with no Bryant and no Gordon, who do you trust the most in the secondary after Johnson? Answer: This is a tough one to answer. Is it Tyrique Stevenson, who has been very inconsistent in his play in the secondary to the point that he lost his job towards the end of the season? Is it Dillon Thieneman, who is a rookie and has never played an NFL snap in his life? Could it possibly be Cam Lewis, who hasn’t consistently been a starter? Or is it Xavier Woods who wasn’t even on the Bears roster until a few weeks ago? I think Thieneman will be the answer within just two or three games into the season, but at this point, I don’t think you can say a rookie who has never taken an NFL snap yet. I certainly don’t think it’s Lewis who I think is the weakest link in the secondary. That leaves Woods and Stevenson. Stevenson has been around the org for over three years, not just three weeks with Woods. But Woods has been a consistent veteran who has started and put in solid performances for multiple organizations. He isn’t a superstar, but he is consistent. Stevenson is anything but consistent. He can make some splash plays, but he has also frequently had lapses and given up major plays against the defense. I think, as crazy as it sounds, I’m picking Woods as the most trustworthy player in the secondary for week one, but as I said, I think Thiemenan takes that title before the calendar turns to October. What do you say, Bears fans? Who do you trust the most in the secondary after Jaylon Johnson? Sound off in the comments below!

title: Chicago Bears Mascot History: From Mr. Bear to Staley Da Bear
summary: The 2026 NFL season marks the 24th year Staley Da Bear will patrol the sidelines. The name Staley drew inspiration from the original moniker of the Chicago Bears. The first iteration of George Halas’s football club started in 1920 as the Decatur Staleys, followed by a single season in 1921 as the Chicago Staleys, before […]
full_text: Frank Dain’s Mr. Bear on left, Staley Da Bear on right The 2026 NFL season marks the 24th year Staley Da Bear will patrol the sidelines. The name Staley drew inspiration from the original moniker of the Chicago Bears. The first iteration of George Halas’s football club started in 1920 as the Decatur Staleys, followed by a single season in 1921 as the Chicago Staleys, before Halas changed the name for the 1922 season to the Chicago Bears. Staley Da Bear harkens back to the start of the Bears— but wait, if Staley arrived on the scene the same year as Charles Tillman and Lance Briggs, what happened in the 80+ years before that? This is the true story of the men dressed in bear mascots with never-before-published photos to give you a glimpse into the distant past. A Real Bearskin Suit In 1935, Frank Conan Dain approached George Halas with an idea. Dain, a former clown in the Ringling Brothers Circus, wanted to roam the sidelines in a bear costume during games to help work the crowd up in support of the team. The former Pittsburgh resident, inspired by the University of Pittsburgh’s Panther, Dain thought a bear would fit right in with the professional circuit. It would mark the first human in a mascot outfit in the pro game. Halas went for it and “Mr. Bear” was born. According to a 1936 article in the Green Bay Press-Gazette , Dain wore a real bearskin suit that ran him $350, about $8,500 in today’s dollars. The suit “hooks up the front and the animal’s chin is strapped to Dain’s own chin so that by opening his mouth Dain can open the bear’s mouth.” According to Don Pierson of the Chicago Tribune , the bear suit “looked fierce. Smelled fierce, too.” Dain enjoyed an incredible run as the Bears mascot, witnessing the NFL’s first dynasty as the team won four championships in seven years in the 1940s. The last of those championships was a 24-14 win over the New York Giants in the Polo Grounds. Dain was there on the sidelines, as captured by this awesome video (you’ll note WGN giving a shout to friend and colleague Jack Silverstein). He was a hit with politicians and celebrities, meeting President Truman in 1953 when he attended a Bears game and singer Patti Page at an armed services event. The final piece of information on Dain’s tenure as Bears mascot appears in a 1954 article by Rocky Wolf in the game program against the Rams on November 28th. Wolf’s short profile of Dain includes a headshot and another photo of Dain in full mascot uniform with a brief bio. The story mentions that Dain, 62 at the time, recently retired from General Motors. That was likely the last season for Dain as the Bears mascot. He would move to Albuquerque for his final eight years, dying at the age of 72. Liz Dain Karzag, granddaughter of Frank, remembers a sweet, kind man who loved to entertain. “His life was like a thick frosting on a cake: full, luscious and messy, but he was as sweet as the frosting and meant good wishing to entertain others and to make them laugh, and he enjoyed that connection with people,” she explained to Windy City Gridiron. He could juggle, walk on his hands, and impersonate famous people of the day. In fact, he won a Charlie Chaplin impersonation contest that took him to Europe to perform. Despite the performance resume and added value Dain delivered on the sidelines Dain Karzag marveled, “You’ll never believe this – George Halas never paid him a single penny.” (Ma’am, that’s the most believable part of the whole story.) Dain performed for the love of the game and the spirit of performance. Exclusive for this story, Liz Dain Karzag shared her personal archives, revealing gem upon gem of Chicago Bears history. Published here for the first time ever are pictures of Dain from the personal archives, including meeting President Truman and singer Patti Page, a famous photo of the 1946 NFL championship game celebration, images from the 1954 program, and so much more. The First Transition, Mic’d Up (For Cryin’ Out Loud!) The second human to roam the Bears sidelines as the mascot was George Motyka, made famous by a memorable NFL Films clip from 1970 and a wonderful behind the scenes feature put out decades later. Working on a #Bears mascot story and this video is amazing stuff. George Motyka pic.twitter.com/d8b6eRmRW0 — Jeff Berckes (Motivated) (@gridironborn) August 18, 2026 The first video contains game footage from a 20-16 victory over the Eagles. If it looks like a weird stadium setup, that’s because it is. The Bears played their home opener at Dyche Stadium, the only NFL game ever played there. 1970 was the last year the Bears called Wrigley Field home, and with the NFL season overlapping with the MLB season in September, the Bears needed a local stadium to host the early-season tilt. The second video is a “behind the scenes” that aired in 2000 from NFL Films. When did Motyka take over as Mr. Bear? Given the timing of the Dain article (late 1954 season), and Motyka’s accounting about running costume ideas by George Halas Jr. (Mugs), 1955 is the earliest possible year. However, Motyka claimed he started 1954 in interviews and his obituary cites 1952. We know from Dain’s obituary that he lived in Albuquerque for eight years before his death in early 1965, which potentially puts him in Chicago as late as 1956 or early 1957. Don Pierson of the Tribune in September of 1983 said Motyka was on the job for 27 years, which would give Motyka a start date of 1956. Given all the evidence, the best bet is the transfer from Dain to Motyka occurred in the 1955 or 1956 season. Motyka recounts the story of talking to the Bears team doctor at the hospital he was working at around that time, asking what happened to the bear (Dain) on the sideline. The doctor didn’t know and apparently suggested Motyka step in. Motyka, a lifelong Bears fan, grew up with Mugs Halas (Motyka was about three years his junior) and his appeal to replace Dain fell on receptive ears despite not bringing any notable performance experience to the job. His costume was approved by Mugs Halas and moved away from the real bearskin Dain favored in the direction of a modern mascot outfit. Just like that, the window washer from O’Hare airport became the second Bears mascot. Motyka’s start date may vary depending on the source (see sidebar) , but his end date is well established. In 1984, when the Bears traveled to San Francisco to take on the 49ers in the NFC Championship game, they left Motyka off the manifest. Word leaked, and the papers picked up the plight of Motyka, causing a bit of a stir. Cook County Board commissioner Charles Bowen spearheaded a fundraising campaign ($25 each from the 17 County Board members) to cover Motyka’s hotel room and meals, while American Airlines offered Motyka a free flight to the City by the Bay. But Motyka stayed home. He wasn’t sure the Bears would let him on the field, and it didn’t seem right to sit in the stands. Motyka said he received supportive calls from everyone with the exception of two people: the President of the United States and Michael McCaskey, Chairman of the Board of the Bears. Without a call from McCaskey, Motyka wouldn’t (and didn’t) go to San Francisco. Motyka, much like his predecessor, was never officially a Bears employee as he wasn’t paid for his services. He enjoyed season tickets with an enviable view and a parking spot right next to George Halas’s for 30 “happy years like part of the family.” With Motyka’s connection to Mugs Halas and, one can imagine, a familial relationship after decades on the sidelines with George Halas, he must have felt like part of the Bears family. By 1984, those relationships may not have been as strong with Mugs dying of a heart attack in 1979 and Papa Bear passing in 1983. Motyka added years later in a 1992 interview with the Chicago Tribune , “I was just shoved out in the cold. I don’t go to the games anymore. I know if I put my name on the waiting list for tickets I’d never get them. It hurts to this day.” Despite…
author: Jeff Berckes

title: Blake Freeland could quickly earn the Bengals’ swing tackle job
summary: On Tuesday, the Cincinnati Bengals finished filling out their 16-player practice squad. They announced three outside additions from other teams, those being offensive tackle Blake Freeland, cornerback Trikweze Bridges, and defensive end Garmon Randolph. Freeland is the most likely to see a path to being called up to the 53-man roster early in the season, […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans cornerback Elijah Molden (24) tries to navigate around Indianapolis Colts offensive tackle Blake Freeland (73) but is unable to get the first down Sunday, Dec. 3, 2023, at Nissan Stadium in Nashville, Tenn. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co On Tuesday, the Cincinnati Bengals finished filling out their 16-player practice squad. They announced three outside additions from other teams, those being offensive tackle Blake Freeland, cornerback Trikweze Bridges, and defensive end Garmon Randolph. Freeland is the most likely to see a path to being called up to the 53-man roster early in the season, with the question marks at the swing tackle spot. Blake Freeland’s Resume Freeland is a 25-year-old who played college football at BYU. He had actually been a quarterback originally for his first couple of seasons in high school before switching to tight end as a junior and senior. At BYU, he switched to the offensive line. That athleticism still showed up when he jumped a 37” vertical at the NFL Scouting Combine, a record that still stands for offensive linemen. Freeland was selected by the Indianapolis Colts in the 4th round of the 2023 NFL Draft. He played in just over 700 snaps during his rookie season. He played in 16 games that season, starting in nine of them. He had starts at both left and right tackle that year. Freeland’s ability to play on either side was likely a selling point for Scott Peters and the rest of the Bengals offensive staff. Went back and watched new Bengals offensive tackle Blake Freeland (#73) as a rookie versus Cincinnati in 2023. pic.twitter.com/zkK79vS2ez — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 1, 2026 Freeland only played in 23 total snaps during his second season with the Colts. Then he fractured his leg in the preseason before the 2025 season began. Freeland did play in 153 snaps during this preseason. He finished with a really impressive 74.5 run-blocking grade per PFF. On the flip side, his pass blocking grade was a 43.1 this preseason. Going back and watching the tape, I haven’t seen it be nearly that bad, so take the pass-blocking grade with a giant grain of salt. Blake Freeland’s (#73) 1st half snaps vs. New England in preseason Week 1. I don’t know Clark, looks pretty good to me.. pic.twitter.com/qJAv7I62BZ — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 1, 2026 Freeland still has some concerns with handling NFL power. Weighing just 302 pounds, his anchor strength consistency is a concern. He does have excellent athleticism, good length with almost 34” arms, and impressive leg drive as a run blocker. The 6’8” Freeland was not claimed off of waivers. Ultimately, he landed in Cincinnati as a member of the practice squad. With actual NFL playing experience at tackle, it wouldn’t be a bit surprising if Freeland ends up being the swing tackle for the Bengals once he is up to speed on the playbook. What are your thoughts on the addition of Blake Freeland? Will he be able to come in and quickly earn the swing tackle spot over Foster, Rivers, and Hinton? Sound off in the comments.

title: Bengals News: No deal for DJ Turner?
summary: NFL insider warns Bengals are on the verge of making a huge mistake before the regular season begins To Turner’s credit, he could have held-in all of training camp looking for a deal. It wouldn’t have even been the wrong move for him. This falls on Cincinnati looking like they will be giving a player […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - OCTOBER 16: DJ Turner II #20 of the Cincinnati Bengals celebrates an interception during the NFL 2025 game between Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on October 16, 2025 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images NFL insider warns Bengals are on the verge of making a huge mistake before the regular season begins To Turner’s credit, he could have held-in all of training camp looking for a deal. It wouldn’t have even been the wrong move for him. This falls on Cincinnati looking like they will be giving a player an extension a year too late again. Maybe turner plays himself out of Cincinnati’s price range as they commit to claiming to be having cap issues. They will also have to potentially pay a breaking out Myles Murphy next season after declining his 5th-year option earlier this offseason. While this is an exciting team for so many reasons, it certainly feels like it could be going into a rough Offseason yet again. Bengals News New Nameplates Mean A New Bengals Locker Room: ‘We’ve Got A Real Chance’ Center and captain Ted Karras looked at the room after Tuesday’ practice and concluded, “We’ve got a real chance. We’ve got to play to it. A deep team. We’ve got to play to it. It’s an easy team to lead. A lot of guys that want to do the right thing all the time. High energy guys, too. One of the toughest (offensive line) rooms I’ve ever been a part of. Comes to work every day and fights through things.” There certainly seems to be a bit more of a buzz than last year. Last year was all about starting fast. Now it is feeling like they have a shot at a ring. Bengals’ Stewart grateful to practice again after knee injury “In that moment I felt like a little, tiny pop,” Stewart said. “I thought it was over. But thankfully God was on my side.” I can not imagine the mental roller coaster a professional athlete goes through in those split seconds as something like this happens. Obviously, your health is the immediate worry, but then it has to creep in that you likely just went from practicing to play a full season of NFL football to spending it rehabbing. Another fortunate break for the player. Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins injury updates from Bengals Week 1 prep All things considered, while the names are big, there’s no overwhelming reason for concern here for Chase or Higgins. Official injury reports will start next week ahead of the Week 1 game against Tampa Bay on September 13. One of those things when you see these guys mentioned as being injured it turns your head and maybe makes your heart skip a beat. Luckily nothing seems serious. NFL News Raiders name Kirk Cousins starting QB to begin 2026 season; top pick Fernando Mendoza backup It will be fun to see this play out. Cousins seems like he still has it to a degree, but at some point the No. 1 overall pick needs to see the field right? Top 10 NFL offenses in 2026? Bears, Bills, Rams headline my projection The Bengals have ranked no lower than eighth in OPPG in all three of Joe Burrow’s healthy seasons, and he hasn’t missed multiple games in consecutive seasons yet. So, by my calculations, Cincinnati is due for a return to the top 10 in 2026! No surprise to see Cincinnati on this list. If Burrow plays in every game it isn’t a question of whether the offense operates at a Top 10 level, it is how high in the Top 10. Cowboys’ Stephen Jones on Pickens, Lamb: Not sure any team can pay two WRs at top of market “I don’t know of any teams that really can pay two top receivers top of the market, so that’s gonna be a real difficult situation as we move forward,” he said. “We’ve managed to figure out how we can do it for this year. If everything works out the way we think it is, [in] which CeeDee and George both have huge years again, then it’ll be a bigger challenge next year.” Apparently the Bengals are the only team who isn’t too cheap to pay their top two wide receivers.

summary: The Cincinnati Bengals saw former second-round pick DJ Turner II have a breakout season in 2025. He showed flashes before a broken collarbone in 2024, but 2025 was a season where Turner started being mentioned alongside the top cornerbacks in the NFL. Good news for Turner is that it happened right before the final season […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Ja'marr Chase (1) and cornerback DJ Turner II (0) collide over a pass, resulting in a leg injury for Chase during Bengals training camp practice at the Paycor Stadium practice facility in downtown Cincinnati on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Cincinnati Bengals saw former second-round pick DJ Turner II have a breakout season in 2025. He showed flashes before a broken collarbone in 2024, but 2025 was a season where Turner started being mentioned alongside the top cornerbacks in the NFL. Good news for Turner is that it happened right before the final season of his rookie contract. 2026 is the final year of his four-year deal, and as a second-round pick, the team does not get a fifth-year option. Turner stated this offseason that he would like to stay in Cincinnati, but would let his agent handle the business side. ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler recently reported that there is “virtually no chance” that the Bengals and Turner get an extension done before Week 1, which is historically the team’s deadline. “Turner is an underrated cover man out of the AFC North, but this deal has virtually no chance to get done before Week 1, barring a massive and unexpected uptick. It isn’t close, and Turner is poised to play out his rookie deal,” Fowler wrote on ESPN . Fowler also mentioned what he feels is the most likely scenario, and it is one Bengals fans may not like. “If Cincinnati follows its own blueprint, it will franchise-tag Turner as it did with another star defensive back, Jessie Bates III, in 2022. Bates had to play on the tag before reaching a four-year deal with the Atlanta Falcons in free agency. Turner will be in line for a large payday in free agency, if he reaches it. But the franchise tag is a real possibility here,” Fowler predicted. Obviously, fans and both parties would like to see a deal come together to avoid the franchise tag drama, but it appears both sides are pretty far apart on a new deal. While Bates got the franchise tag and then walked, the Bengals did franchise tag Tee Higgins twice and got a long-term extension knocked out last offseason. The Bengals may simply say “Do it again” to Turner and reward him after, but it appears we are a season or two away from knowing the final result.

title: Bengals film room: Offensive rookies vs. Eagles
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Philadelphia Eagles 30-13 in their third and final preseason game of the year. Now, we’re taking a look at how the offensive rookies performed in Philly. Connor Lew Lew was the Bengals’ first selection on the offensive side of the ball this past draft. While that didn’t come until the […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals defeated the Philadelphia Eagles 30-13 in their third and final preseason game of the year. Now, we’re taking a look at how the offensive rookies performed in Philly. Connor Lew Lew was the Bengals’ first selection on the offensive side of the ball this past draft. While that didn’t come until the 4th round, Lew was widely projected as a top-50 prospect before tearing his ACL in late October of 2025. While he is still regaining his form, he showed he has a really bright future in the Queen City. There were a couple of bad reps where he struggled handling pure power, but I chalk that up to still getting back to full strength. Overall, it was another quality performance from the recently turned 21-year-old rookie. Lew played 33 snaps during his second preseason action of the year. That was important for him to show that he can handle starting the season on the active roster. While Lew may not be asked to play a ton this season, he is incredible depth and a player that is set to be the center of the future in Cincinnati. Connor Lew looked good again on Friday night versus the Eagles. Just turned 21 years old today (Happy Birthday) and is the center of the future in Cincinnati. pic.twitter.com/mbh4QIwdwG — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 30, 2026 Colbie Young The Bengals’ second fourth-round draft selection, Young didn’t impress nearly as much as he did during the first couple of preseason games. He finished with just 1 reception for 9 yards on the night. He played in 19 total snaps, which were 10 more than fellow wide receiver Dohnte Meyers. Meyers ended up with 3 catches for 51 yards on his 9 snaps. Colbie Young is still a big part of the future here, but I can see him being a game-day inactive early in the season. The reason being that Meyers has earned a larger role over him to start the season. Regardless, both players will get opportunities throughout the year. It will be up to them to make the most of it. Brian Parker II Parker was the Bengals’ sixth-round draft selection out of Duke this year. He played mainly right tackle for the Blue Devils, but has transitioned to the interior offensive line in Cincinnati. I thought he shined throughout the preseason. He showed his versatility by playing significant snaps at both left and right guard, along with playing some center during the first week of the preseason. Unfortunately, Parker was rolled up on late in the preseason finale. The Bengals decided to place him on IR to begin the season. This means he will miss at least the first four weeks of the season to begin the year. While that is a bummer for him, it doesn’t change his long-term projection in Cincinnati. This is a player who will likely be next in line to start at right guard whenever Dalton Risner’s time in Cincinnati is over. The future looks really bright with an interior offensive line trio of Dylan Fairchild, Connor Lew, and Brian Parker II. Brian Parker II has taken extensive snaps at both left and right guard this preseason. Also, he had some playing time at center during the first week. Valuable depth and a future starter in my opinion. What a steal to land him in the 6th round. pic.twitter.com/bLkqwBMijZ — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 30, 2026 Jack Endries It was another quiet game for Endries on Friday night. He finished the game with just 2 catches for 11 yards. While there were some concerns he could be squeezed off of the 53-man roster, the Bengals elected to keep him as the 5th tight end on Sunday night. I think Endries will be a big part of the future at the tight end position, but he is still coming along as a blocker. For that reason, I think we will see Endries start the season as a game-day inactive early in the year. Jamal Haynes Haynes and fellow undrafted free agent running back Kentrel Bullock were both impressive for the Bengals during the preseason finale. Bullock had 14 carries for 85 yards and scored a touchdown during the game. Haynes finished with 7 carries for 78 yards and a score of his own. I chose to highlight Haynes for this one. He looked extremely shifty in the open field. He is built naturally low to the ground, and his footwork is so fun to watch. The converted wide receiver adds value as a pass catcher and displayed good vision throughout the night. It was an electric performance to end the preseason. Sadly, Haynes was not kept on the 53-man roster and has not been signed to the practice squad, so he’s a free agent. Jamal Haynes was ELECTRIC against the Eagles last night. He ran for 78 yards and a touchdown. Averaging 11.1 yards per carry. He was patient, elusive, and displayed good vision. A player I liked as a former receiver, that should be able to develop into an all-around talent at… pic.twitter.com/7jObSzTsj5 — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 29, 2026

title: Browns 1st quarter schedule: Finding the most likely win
summary: It could be a long season ahead for the Cleveland Browns, but those first few weeks can go a long way toward setting the tone for what the rest of the season will look like. The Browns have a pretty favorable schedule overall, but they’ll have some tough matchups to deal with early in the season. Cleveland’s first home game in […]
full_text: It could be a long season ahead for the Cleveland Browns, but those first few weeks can go a long way toward setting the tone for what the rest of the season will look like. The Browns have a pretty favorable schedule overall , but they’ll have some tough matchups to deal with early in the season. Cleveland’s first home game in Week 3 against the Carolina Panthers is likely their most winnable game in the first quarter. The Panthers finished 8-9 in 2025, compared to the Browns’ opening matchup, the Jacksonville Jaguars, who finished 13-4 last season. The Week 2 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers will also be a challenge for several reasons. The Buccaneers have been one of the NFL’s more competitive teams in recent years, and this one won’t be easy with the Browns heading on the road to face Baker Mayfield – a matchup that comes with plenty of history. The pressure of that matchup alone could make things more challenging. The home environment in Week 3 should also work in the Browns’ favor, with an energized crowd giving the team a boost on both sides of the ball. On that same note, the Week 4 Thursday Night Football matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers is another opportunity for the team to get a win. While those AFC North matchups are always competitive, Cleveland has had some success against the Steelers in Thursday Night Football over the years. Games against Pittsburgh are always unpredictable, so a win is certainly not a guarantee. title: Cleveland Browns have a strategy that may just be crazy enough to work
summary: There are a lot of things to say when talking about the Cleveland Browns. Very old fans can reminisce about how the franchise was once one of the league’s dynasties, led by the father of the modern NFL in head coach Paul Brown. But with their last NFL championship coming in 1964, those memories grow […]
full_text: November 20, 2011; Cleveland, OH , USA; Fans during the game between the Cleveland Browns and the Jacksonville Jaguars at Cleveland Browns Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric P. Mull-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect There are a lot of things to say when talking about the Cleveland Browns. Very old fans can reminisce about how the franchise was once one of the league’s dynasties, led by the father of the modern NFL in head coach Paul Brown. But with their last NFL championship coming in 1964, those memories grow dimmer every year. Those of us who are old, but not that old, can share tales of the teams of the 1980s, perennial playoff participants that reached the cusp of the Super Bowl three times under the franchise’s last great head coach in Marty Schottenheimer and everyone’s favorite quarterback in Bernie Kosar. For today’s fans, those teams may as well have played in the leather helmet era; it was so long ago. And while they have been able to cheer for some of the franchise’s most legendary players like Joe Thomas, Nick Chubb, Myles Garrett, and Joel Bitonio, that has not always been a comfort once the game ended on another lost Sunday afternoon. That is because, of all the things one could say about the Browns, the one thing they have not been able to say much since 1999 is that the team plays winning football. Such is life when you are a team that has made just three playoff appearances in 27 seasons, has just four winning seasons, and has had 10 or more losses in 19 seasons. That is a sobering sentence to write, and not one that will fill the hearts of fans – or seats at the new stadium in a few years – with the regular season just 11 days away. But fear not, Browns Nation, because the team appears to be finally building a solid foundation with a productive draft class in 2025 and what looks to be an even better one in 2026. (Just set aside the quarterback situation until next year. Because the Browns certainly have.) Unlike in years past, when draft picks were squandered on the likes of Johnny Manziel, Justin Gilbert, Brian Robiskie, Chaun Thompson, Nate Orchard, and countless other players, the situation is looking promising because the Browns have a plan in place. And what is that plan, you ask? It is all about trying to win football games! That is according to assistant general manager and vice president of football operations Catherine Hickman, who had her turn with the media on Wednesday. While she was asked specifically about head coach Todd Monken’s decision to name Deshaun Watson as the starting quarterback, her answer addressed the organization’s current approach : “Everything we do is to win football games. That’s how we make our decisions, that’s how we think about it as an organization, and that’s no different at that position.” You know what? That is a plan that is just crazy enough to work! Before we go any further, that is not a shot at Hickman in any way because she likely gets more than her share of garbage simply for being a female in a male-dominated business. But it is a bit of an odd answer, because isn’t that the entire purpose of an NFL team? To win? (Unless you are the owner, then the purpose is to continue to print money, and if wins come along, that is a happy bonus.) Because if you have to tell people that you are actively trying to win football games, it is probably because it is not readily apparent that is the plan. At least now we know there is organizational alignment toward a common path. And anytime the Browns want to get busy actually winning some games, there is a long-suffering fan base ready and waiting.

title: Browns practice schedule is interesting heading into Week 1
summary: There is nothing normal about the NFL anymore. What used to be a clear schedule, with clear roster and practice schedules, has devolved into almost anarchy. Rosters used to be cut down slowly but surely through the offseason. Now, a Sunday night cutdown from 90 players to the initial 53-man roster. The NFL season kicks […]
full_text: Aug 4, 2026; Berea, OH, USA; Cleveland Browns head coach Todd Monken talks to the team during training camp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus. Mandatory Credit: Ken Blaze-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect There is nothing normal about the NFL anymore. What used to be a clear schedule, with clear roster and practice schedules, has devolved into almost anarchy. Rosters used to be cut down slowly but surely through the offseason. Now, a Sunday night cutdown from 90 players to the initial 53-man roster . The NFL season kicks off with a Wednesday game… WEDNESDAY! Then it is followed by a Thursday game, which would be normal, except that the game is in Melbourne, Australia. A wild and unusual start to the 2026 NFL season indeed. For the Cleveland Browns, the start to the season and their schedule are as normal as it gets: Sunday, 1 PM, right down the ticket, except for a To Be Determined Week 18 matchup. The big difference is the two weeks between roster cutdowns and Week 1. Due to that, Browns players now have a few days off from practice with nothing scheduled until Monday, then the normal practice schedule starting on Wednesday. With how much players use social media, it will be interesting to see which ones post any trips they have planned for this little break, or does everyone stay near Berea after a grueling, hot training camp? Hopefully the Cleveland roster spends the downtime doing exactly what they need to do in order to be prepared for Week 1, as fans also get to take a breather and prepare for what is to come in the 2026 season.

title: Recent moves show the Cowboys finally get something important
summary: A lot has happened over the last week. The Dallas Cowboys, like every NFL team, officially set their 53-man roster. As is usually the case this was an initial version of it because of various adjustments that had to be made. We saw that play itself out with the waiving of Joe Milton, the claiming […]
full_text: OXNARD, CA - JULY 28: Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones listens as head coach Brian Schottenheimer answers a question during an opening press conference at training camp on Tuesday, July 28, 2026, in Oxnard, Calif. (Smiley N. Pool/The Dallas Morning News via Getty Images) A lot has happened over the last week. The Dallas Cowboys, like every NFL team, officially set their 53-man roster. As is usually the case this was an initial version of it because of various adjustments that had to be made. We saw that play itself out with the waiving of Joe Milton, the claiming of Emari Demarcado, and before either of those the trades involving Broderick Jones (in) and Nate Thomas (out). Roster cuts are often an emotional experience for people. When your pet cat makes it you feel like you won the lottery. The other side of that coin is that when he is cut you feel personally impacted. Dallas entered that period with a high approval rate for recent moves, but some of their cuts maybe burned a bit of it up. Given that the Broderick Jones trade was not well-received from a compensation standpoint and some of the proverbial wind has been lost behind the sails. As we have had a few days to sit on it, I have come to a realization personally: I am great with all of this. How many times have we talked about how notoriously inactive the Cowboys are in certain aspects of roster-building? Think of all of the years we have implored them to be more active in these types of areas. When you swing over and over and over again you are going to realize that batting 1.000 is tough work. We are looking for .300 here, a respectable mark, and more than anything the willingness to keep getting in the box. For all we know the Broderick Jones trade could even work out wonderfully and the C grade it received won’t even matter. In the aftermath of that deal there was some mild panic about Dallas having only four draft picks (quantitatively speaking) for next year, and you know what? I also love that. I love that the Cowboys were not averse to the deal because it would leave them shy for 2027 (they did pick up a seventh a day after the Jones trade by dealing Nate Thomas). I love that they, seemingly, trust themselves to figure it out when that time comes. The time at the moment pertains to 2026 and they have to stand in and take pitches, and most importantly they have to swing at the ones they like. Being shy about them because of how it might impact their batting average or what it could mean for the next at-bat, or heck even next season’s, isn’t prudent. Everything about this season continues to remain a breath of fresh air. Famous last words and all of that for obvious reasons, but right now this team seems to get it in some of the most important ways.
