With Seattle on “Hard Knocks” and the Rams making splash after splash this offseason, the Eagles are about as under the radar as can be. Reminder: […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - AUGUST 04: Philadelphia Eagles offensive coordinator Sean Mannion looks on during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on August 4th, 2026 at Jefferson Health Training Center in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … NFL execs rank NFC teams: Rams, Seahawks clear favorites. Can the Bears keep rising? – The Athletic 3) PHILADELPHIA EAGLES. With Seattle on “Hard Knocks” and the Rams making splash after splash this offseason, the Eagles are about as under the radar as can be. Reminder: Philly leads the league in regular-season victories over the past four seasons (50) while ranking second to Kansas City in postseason wins (six). “They could go either way, to be quite honest,” one exec said of the Eagles, who finished 11-6 last season. “I think they will be better. The thing that was really good for them is a potential concern, and that is the receiver position and running back. Saquon (Barkley) did not have a great year. The offensive line health and age is a concern. They will still be formidable.” Will A.J. Brown’s departure be addition by subtraction? One voter said the pressure’s on quarterback Jalen Hurts, whose relationship with Brown had grown cold and who will be playing in an overhauled offensive system under new coordinator Sean Mannion. “It was hard for me to ding Philly even if the offense is unknown, even if they are taking a step back without A.J. Brown,” another exec said. “Vic Fangio and that defense is going to be top five. That O-line is going to be pretty good. It is still Saquon Barkley. Could they win 16-13 every week? Probably.” Eagles Film Review: Analyzing Makai Lemon’s debut and other 53-man roster inclusions – BGN Makai Lemon’s first appearance was hardly spectacular. He caught three of his five targets for three yards, was targeted on Tanner McKee’s interception, and muffed a punt late in the game. However, I am not going to panic about a first-round receiver after one preseason appearance. I did not dislike this first route as much when I watched the All-22. On the TV copy, the release looked slow, but it looks better from a wide angle. Lemon has never been an outstanding separator against press coverage, and probably never will be, but his work at the line of scrimmage is good here. He beats the initial contact, gets on top of the cornerback, and puts himself in a position to win vertically. The problem comes at the top of the route. Lemon looks inside without selling the possibility that he is actually breaking in that direction, allowing the cornerback to read the route and make a play on the football. Obviously, it’s only one rep, but Lemon must become better at manipulating defensive backs once he has established leverage. Simply looking in one direction will not move NFL cornerbacks consistently. Still, arguably the difficult part of this rep is defeating press coverage and stacking the defender. Lemon does that well. It wasn’t an ideal debut, but it wasn’t a disastrous one. Connect with other NFL fans on the new SB Nation app – SB Nation It’s such an exciting time here at SB Nation with our launch of a brand-new, free app! You’ve probably seen the links at the bottom of your screen, with availability on both iOS and Android, but I want to explain a little about why the app is going to be a daily read for you. Firstly, the home screen, which is a rolling feed of everything you tell us you want to see. We understand fans, and that being hyper-focused on just your city is what a lot of you care about, so this strips out all the extra stuff to only show you what you want to see. Conversely, some of you like a broader picture of the entire league. Here you can follow NFL as an entire community, where we’ll break down stories with national significance and importantly, allow you to find like-minded, engaged sports fans who want to talk about the big stories in football every day. Community is at the heart of this, as we bring together our vast network of team sites and national coverage all into one place. 🚨🚨🚨 SB Nation has an app! 🚨🚨🚨 The new, FREE SB Nation app is the best way to follow the sites you already love and connect with fans in new communities! You also get: – Fewer ads – An easier way to read and comment – A championship for your favorite team [not a guarantee] pic.twitter.com/YK2LEMeu9t — SB Nation (@SBNation) September 1, 2026 30 Eagles training camp questions, answered – PhillyVoice The answer to the question posed here is no, Makai Lemon did not earn a starting role. He missed most of camp with a hamstring injury, and when he did practice he didn’t stand out. Also, his lone preseason game was a dud, as he had 3 catches for 3 yards on 5 targets, including a drop that led to an INT, and a muffed punt. That said, he might start anyway. Smith will be the WR1, and Dontayvion Wicks will be the WR2. When Lemon was ready to practice after a long period of being out, he was inserted right back into the starting lineup. Many of the other wide receivers had better camps than Lemon, but not to the degree that they should be no-brainer starters. So, we’ll see. My guess is that the Eagles will shoehorn him into the starting lineup Week 1, as the WR3. Behind the Eagles’ group effort to not let Makai Lemon fall behind – NBCSP “With Makai, we had to come up with creative ways to get him walkthroughs and to get him different things that he could do while he was out,” Eagles receivers coach Aaron Moorehead said on Tuesday. “He couldn’t physically run but we could walk through things or we could talk through things and we could have him break the huddle and go where he needed to go just to catch him up that way. It wasn’t the most fun thing in the world. I know he wanted to be out there and I know we all wanted him to be out there but that’s what you do. You sacrifice your time and you sacrifice your energy to get where you want to go. For the short term, it’s, ‘Hey, let’s get to Washington.’ But long-term, it’s like, ‘Where are we going to be at the end of the year?’ He took it really well and I thought that it was a collaborative effort.” Moorehead gave credit to Howie Roseman, Nick Sirianni, Parks Frazier, the entire coaching staff and players for helping to make sure Lemon would be able to be quickly reintegrated when he returned from the injury. More on the Practice Squad and Roster – Iggles Blitz I wonder if the decision to keep Elijah Moore and Jonathan Jones was influenced by last year being a disappointment. Maybe that team needed less focus on potential and more on results. This roster certainly feels more results oriented. Howie said Moore had a great camp. You want to reward that with a roster spot. Keeping Bernard over him might have sent the wrong message to the team. The Eagles went with the player who earned it. They kept EJ Jenkins because he had a good summer. I was crazy enough to rewatch part of the Cincy game. Jenkins blocking stood out to me. That requires effort and physicality. Jenkins got rewarded for being a good blue collar player. Good for him and Moore. This team should be hungry after the disappointing end to 2025 and the offseason changes. AJ Brown is gone. Jeff Stoutland is gone. Adoree Jackson is gone (just seeing if you’re paying attention). They aren’t running last year back. This is a different team. I think the roster moves reflect a different mentality. The projects went to the practice squad so they’re still part of the organization and the future. They just didn’t get roster spots like we expected. I’m glad the team was able to bring back Bernard and Weru. I still believe in them. Jalen Hurts’ GQ interview shows us an Eagles QB who was never going to accede to A.J. title: Steelers sign former Titans safety, round out practice squad
summary: By announcing the signing of safety Bishop Fitzgerald on Wednesday, the Steelers have officially filled all 17 spots on their 2026 practice squad ahead of the regular season. According to Steelers.com, the initial squad is as follows, with outside linebacker Julius Welschof filling the International Player Pathway Program exemption slot: Steelers 2026 practice squad Three […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 30: Bishop Fitzgerald #19 of the USC Trojans scores a touchdown after intercepting a pass against the Missouri State Bears during the second quarter at United Airlines Field at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on August 30, 2025 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images By announcing the signing of safety Bishop Fitzgerald on Wednesday, the Steelers have officially filled all 17 spots on their 2026 practice squad ahead of the regular season. According to Steelers.com, the initial squad is as follows, with outside linebacker Julius Welschof filling the International Player Pathway Program exemption slot: Steelers 2026 practice squad DL Kyler Baugh S Sebastian Castro S Bishop Fitzgerald RB Travis Homer WR Max Hurleman WR Brandon Johnson OL Steven Jones TE Lake McRee OL Doug Nester RB Lew Nichols DL Esezi Otomewo CB Doneiko Slaughter WR Brandon Smith LB Bradyn Swinson CB Car’lin Vigers OLB Julius Welschof (International Player Pathway Program exemption) LB Jacoby Windmon Three players: Fitzgerald, Swinson and Vigers, are new to the Steelers organization. Fitzgerald was an undrafted free agent in 2026, spending the summer with the Tennessee Titans. Playing college football at NC State and USC, Fitzgerald recorded his best collegiate seasons in 2025 with the Trojans, when he logged five interceptions alongside 51 total tackles. The 5’11, 201-pound safety ran a 4.55-second 40-yard dash at the NFL Combine. Pre-draft, NFL.com analyst Lance Zierlein described Fitzgerald as a “compact, ballhawking safety prospect with alignment versatility,” noting he’s much better defending the pass than diagnosing the run. Vigers went undrafted in 2025 out of UL Monroe, spending time on the Washington Commanders’ practice squad last season. In his final collegiate season in 2024, the 6’2, 200-pound corner logged 38 total tackles and one interception. He scored an 8.00 RAS with a reported 4.52-second 40-yard dash. Swinson is the most interesting name of the bunch as a former fifth-round pick by the New England Patriots in 2025. He appeared in three games for the Patriots last season, recording one tackle. In his final collegiate season at LSU in 2024, he recorded 8.5 sacks along with 59 total tackles. Zierlein described Swinson as a “late bloomer with big hands, long arms and a frame to carry more muscle” pre-draft, adding he’s “competitive at the point of attack, where he uses his length and footwork to beat the block or prevent block sustains.” Zierlein noted Swinson still needed to work on rushing strategies and improving quickness, but had the upside to be a starting outside linebacker in a 3-4. Interestingly, the Steelers’ initial practice squad does not include the reported signing of former Cowboys safety Juanyeh Thomas. The planned deal was reported by ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler on Monday, and seemingly confirmed by Thomas making a string of Steelers-related posts on X afterwards. For now, Thomas is not listed on Pittsburgh’s roster or practice squad. Thomas reportedly visited with the Steelers Wednesday.

title: Aaron Rodgers continues to praise Steelers young pass catchers
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers made it a point of emphasis this offseason to add to their wide receiver room. Last season, it felt like too much of the pressure fell on the shoulders of DK Metcalf. After trading for Michal Pittman Jr, drafting Germie Bernard, and having another offseason to continue to develop Roman Wilson, the […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Head coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers talks with Aaron Rodgers #8 prior to the game against the Green Bay Packers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers made it a point of emphasis this offseason to add to their wide receiver room. Last season, it felt like too much of the pressure fell on the shoulders of DK Metcalf. After trading for Michal Pittman Jr, drafting Germie Bernard, and having another offseason to continue to develop Roman Wilson, the Steelers’ receiver room has a much more positive outlook for 2026. Speaking to the media after practice Wednesday, Rodgers took time to talk about a mistake that Wilson made in practice that resulted in an interception. “Roman made a repeat mistake,” Rodgers told the media . “That’s a good learning experience, because I don’t think he’s going to do that again. But he did the same thing early in training camp, and we said, ‘hey, on that under route, you’ve got to keep coming.’ So I think it’s best that it happened in practice. Roman is a great kid. He’s had a fantastic camp. I have utmost confidence in him. He’s going to have to play a big role for us. But mistakes can happen. That’s a great one to happen in practice. But he’s gotten a lot better, and I’m really proud of Roman.” Despite Wilson making a “repeat mistake” today is practice, I think it’s telling that Rodgers took the time to express just how much confidence he has in him. Wilson was a healthy scratch in four of the last five regular season games last season, so it’s hard to imagine Rodgers trusted him last season. After putting together a second really impressive training camp, it seems like the bond between Rodgers and Wilson has grown over the offseason. When Rodgers was asked about how rookie second round pick Germie Bernard has looked throughout the preseason, he praised the young wideouts attention to detail. “He’s got a great attitude. He really wants to learn. The best thing I can say about him is he hasn’t made repeat mistakes. There’s mistakes that are going to happen as part of the game, especially for young guys,” Rodgers said. “But when he does make a mistake, he takes it to heart and studies it and makes sure he doesn’t repeat that thing.” After saying that Wilson made a “repeat mistake,” I find it interesting that Rodgers used the same wording when describing the rookie wideout. Rodgers has a tendency to not trust young players as much, so the fact that he’s saying that Bernard learns and adapts quickly form his mistakes is crucial. The veteran quarterback knows the young wideouts could be a big part of the Steelers’ passing attack in 2026. In what could be a more pass-heavy offense under new head coach Mike McCarthy, the more players Rodgers trusts to get the ball to, the better. Let us know what you think in the comments . full_text: The Pittsburgh Steelers’ ongoing saga with Joey Porter Jr. doesn’t appear to be ending anytime soon. The team and their star cornerback don’t appear to be anywhere near agreeing on a long-term extension, which has led to the Penn State product sitting out all of training camp and preseason. Now, ESPN NFL insider Jeremy Fowler is reporting that Porter could request a trade from the team, as well as sit out games, should that be the route he decides to go. “Sources say the Steelers’ lack of a formal offer for weeks sent the clear message to Porter that they would like him to play out the final year of his rookie contract, which prompted him to consider the possibility of a trade or sitting out for an extended period,” Fowler writes . “The 26-year-old stayed away from the practice field for weeks but returned Tuesday. Perhaps his participation ignites talks, but he’s leaving that up to his agents.” Porter himself hinted at the possibility of sitting out games when speaking to the media on Tuesday. ”I have to talk to the guys upstairs, my agents about that one,” Porter said when asked if he would play Week 1. The Steelers don’t negotiate contracts once the season begins, something that Omar Khan confirmed won’t change , meaning they have a hard deadline to get something done with Porter. The more this drags out, though, the more speculation will come on a potential parting of ways. Let us know what you think in the comments . summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers traded former first-round pick Broderick Jones to the Dallas Cowboys on Saturday. It also came after the Steelers declined to pick […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 21: Broderick Jones #77 of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks on during the game against the New York Jets at Acrisure Stadium on August 21, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers traded former first-round pick Broderick Jones to the Dallas Cowboys on Saturday. This came off the heels of the Georgia product playing deep into preseason games as he worked his way back from a neck injury and missed the entirety of spring workouts. It also came after the Steelers declined to pick up his fifth-year option and drafted his replacement in the form of Max Iheanachor. Once that sequence of actions happened, Jones’ days in Pittsburgh were numbered. Jones spoke to the media for the first time as a member of the Cowboys and was asked what he believed didn’t work with him and the Steelers. “For me, I would just say bouncing around, just not being able to get my feet set,” Jones said via John Machota of The Athletic. “That was a challenge for me. Coming in [to Dallas], hopefully I can stick to one side. Compete for that, get comfortable, get familiar with it, get familiar with who I’ll be playing next to and go from there.” Jones originally replaced Chuks Okorafor at right tackle in 2023 and spent the entire 2024 season at that spot. In 2025, he moved to left tackle after the Steelers drafted Troy Fautanu. He played both right and left tackle in preseason this year. Now, Jones will compete with Terrance Steele to be the Cowboys starting right tackle, while the Steelers will roll forward with Fautanu, Iheanachor, and Dylan Cook as their offensive tackles. title: Biggest surprises  and questions from the Steelers’ initial 53-man roster
summary: Real football is almost here. The preseason has come to an end, and we’re just 11 days from the Steelers kicking off their season at home against the Atlanta Falcons. Before the season could begin, each team had to make cuts to comply with the 53-man roster limit. Read & React made our roster predictions […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 21: Head coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers talks with Drew Allar #16 and Will Howard #18 prior to the game against the New York Jets at Acrisure Stadium on August 21, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images Real football is almost here. The preseason has come to an end, and we’re just 11 days from the Steelers kicking off their season at home against the Atlanta Falcons. Before the season could begin, each team had to make cuts to comply with the 53-man roster limit. Read & React made our roster predictions last week, and while we got quite a bit right, as always, there were a few moves we didn’t see coming. Let’s dive into how the first active roster of the season shaped out. RB : It was expected to be a fairly straightforward roster cutdown day this season, but there were a few curveballs that kept things interesting. Ryan, what did you find the most surprising? RP : I think the trades were the most surprising part of the process. The Kaleb Johnson one wasn’t too shocking, I suppose. We both predicted he wouldn’t make the roster, after all. In Pittsburgh, Johnson didn’t flash the glimpses of potential that got him drafted in the third round, and the new offense no longer tailored to his presumed skillset. While his time here was disappointing, it does make sense that a team would be willing to throw the Steelers a late Day 3 pick to take a chance on a running back with Johnson’s draft pedigree. The real surprise was the Broderick Jones trade. I didn’t think any team would be interested in a tackle that has largely disappointed and is coming off a neck injury. Broderick’s showing in the preseason was also a pretty tough watch. The Steelers trade with Dallas can essentially be broken down as upgrading a fourth-round pick into a third-round pick, and then swapping Jones for a sixth-round pick. It’s safe to call him a failed first pick, for general manager Omar Khan, but I do like that the Steelers are turning the situation into future assets rather than letting Jones ride out a lame-duck final year of his contract. One development I think we could say wasn’t so surprising was the Steelers deciding to keep four quarterbacks on the roster. I suspect you and I share similar apprehensions about this decision, Ryland, but we can’t truly call this a surprise after the team spent most of the preseason soft launching this concept. As of now, they do appear prepared to carry on with this plan, as they did not claim anyone off waivers, nor have they signed any free agents onto the active roster. What are your thoughts on the viability of this plan? RB : I think there are some valid reasons for and against the Steelers keeping four quarterbacks on their initial 53-man roster – I’ll emphasize the “initial” here – but it still stands out as an unorthodox roster-building move. Ultimately, I still think there’s a solid chance this is a piece of roster calculus before the regular season like what happened last year . Maybe the team wants to sneak Howard onto the practice squad after the initial wave of waiver claims. There has also been reported trade interest in Mason Rudolph that the Steelers didn’t act on before cutdowns because of the compensation. Could they be waiting for a better deal? That said, Mike McCarthy made it no secret how much he likes the Steelers’ four quarterbacks this offseason, so it’s difficult to rule out this roster choice being a year-long decision. However, by the time mid-season roster churn hits we won’t be as up in arms about the choice to leave a fifth-string linebacker or fourth-string safety off the 53-man roster, especially with practice squad elevations, but it’s hard to deny this is a rather strange roster strategy considering the quarterback room Pittsburgh has. RP : I’m not so sure we won’t be if injuries start to take a toll, or if we have some special teams gaffes, but we’ll touch more on that in a bit. Oddly enough, the Steelers aren’t the only team bucking NFL norms and carrying four quarterbacks to start the season. Who else is doing this, and do they have any compelling reasons for why? RB : I’ve seen the stat that three other teams also kept four passers initially as a way of proving Pittsburgh’s decision wasn’t that out of the ordinary (hardly a majority of NFL teams, especially considering 12 only kept two quarterbacks initially), but it’s worth pointing out those three other teams had much better reasoning than the Steelers. To recap: The Falcons (Tua Tagovailoa, Michael Penix Jr., Cooper Rush, Jack Strand) have two injury-prone starters and lots of quarterback questions this year. The Eagles (Jalen Hurts, Andy Dalton, Tanner McKee, Cole Payton) have a Taysom Hill-lite in their rookie QB4 who contributed on special teams in the preseason, plus they’ve got a fairly long-standing track record of trading quarterbacks. And the Vikings (Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz, J.J. McCarthy, Max Brosmer) seem to just be waiting for the right trade package for McCarthy. The Steelers, on the other hand, have a proven starter in Aaron Rodgers, and Mason Rudolph, Will Howard and Drew Allar are not going to be seeing snaps on gameday unless Rodgers gets hurt or it’s garbage time. RP : I think that last point is one of my major hang-ups with this as a roster construction strategy. The biggest, naturally from our outside perspective, is that keeping four quarterbacks feels like the Steelers failing to commit to a plan. The team’s messaging presents a team that says it wants to be competitive this year for their older defensive core and their starting quarterback on his farewell tour. And yet many of the moves they have made over the past several months feel like a team trying to also hold space for its younger players. This quarterback decision – or, one might argue, a failure to make a hard decision – feels like the Steelers once again refusing to lean into either strategy fully. Instead, the Steelers are trying to straddle two lanes at once: competing and developing for the future. But rather than getting the best of both worlds, I worry they’re shortchanging themselves on both fronts. This feels even more potent at the quarterback position. There just aren’t a ton of reps the backups get during the season. One of the three passers behind Rodgers will be in charge of running scout team quarterback. This can be a useful opportunity to develop a young passer, but that is limited if the team is splitting those reps each week between the three backups, or changing who runs the scout team based on the opponent for a given week. It also makes me question: Does having four passers in the room help with developing a young passer’s mental side of the game because it adds more perspective, or does it dilute it due to forming a reliance on having an extra person to divvy up the week’s preparation responsibilities to? I’m not pretending to know the answer to that, but I am curious about it. RB : Speaking of the emphasis on holding space for younger players, all 10 of the Steelers’ draft picks this year made the initial 53, as well as a surprise 11th in undrafted defensive lineman Kevin Jobity Jr. While the Steelers had plenty of roster spots for that rookie class to fill this offseason, it’s genuinely impressive that all made the team. Only one member of the draft class, Eli Heidenreich, wasn’t seen as a near-lock for the roster ahead of cutdown, and even the seventh-round running back certainly made a clear case for the spot he earned in the team’s final preseason game. Heidenreich clearly has more burst as a runner than the consensus RB3 candidate at the time, Travis Homer, and showed off some good, decisive running and even a little bit of power against the Bills. More importantly, he logged a special teams kickoff tackle, saw reps as the personal protector on the punt team, and looks like a capable return man to back up fellow rookie Kaden Wetjen. This guy…

full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: A.J. Brown #1 of the New England Patriots warms up prior to an NFL preseason football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots are set for a Super Bowl rematch next Wednesday at Lumen Field. While Patriots fans are hoping for some measure of revenge, neutrals are probably hoping this game is a little more dramatic and competitive than the Super Bowl proved to be. What we do know is that there have been some high-profile roster changes for both teams. There’s no need to rehash the Seahawks’ departures and additions because, well, there weren’t that many changes, plus we’re a Seahawks site obligated to cover every morsel of news. But what about the Patriots? The AFC champions made some major moves at wide receiver, but what else have they’ve done? Let’s look at who the Patriots lost and gained since the Super Bowl, with an emphasis on outgoing players who actually played meaningful snaps in Santa Clara. Notable New England Patriots departures Garrett Bradbury is no longer the starting center , having been traded to the center-needy Chicago Bears after Drew Dalman retired. Fullback Jack Westover was released during roster cuts and has since signed with the Washington Commanders practice squad. Starting wide receiver Stefon Diggs was released and is now with the Washington Commanders. Wide receiver Kayshon Boutte was traded in preseason to the wide receiver-needy Houston Texans, who lost Jayden Higgins for the season to a torn ACL. Boutte was second in touchdown receptions behind Stefon Diggs and third among wide receivers in catches. Reserve tight end Austin Hooper signed with his original drafting team, the Atlanta Falcons, in free agency. Hooper was TE2 behind Hunter Henry. Starting safety Jaylinn Hawkins signed with the Baltimore Ravens in free agency. Outside linebacker Anfernee Jennings was released and signed with the New Orleans Saints. Jennings was a rotational player (280 regular season defensive snaps). Starting outside linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson signed with the Washington Commanders as a free agent. Inside linebacker Jack Gibbens signed with the Arizona Cardinals in free agency. Gibbens started half the season and played defensive snaps in every game. Inside linebacker Jahlani Tavai was released and has since signed with the Jacksonville Jaguars. Tavai was a rotational backer who was one of New England’s leading special teams guys in snaps played. Defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga agreed to a three-year contract with the Kansas City Chiefs in free agency. Tonga played a career-high 337 snaps in a rotation with Milton Williams and Christian Barmore. Notable New England Patriots arrivals Wide receiver A.J. Brown was acquired in a big trade with the Philadelphia Eagles. Wide receiver Romeo Doubs signed a four-year contract as a free agent. Fullback Reggie Gilliam joined as a free agent from the Buffalo Bills. Starting left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker signed a three-year deal in free agency. Starting safety Kevin Byard signed a one-year contract in free agency. Outside linebacker and former Seahawk Dre’Mont Jones signed a three-year contract in free agency. New England Patriots rostered 2026 draft picks Round 1, pick 28: Right tackle Caleb Lomu Round 2, pick 55 : EDGE Gabe Jacas Round 3, pick 95 : Tight end Eli Raridon Round 5, pick 171 : Cornerback Karon Prunty Round 6, pick 196 : Left tackle Dametrious Crownover Round 6, pick 212 : Linebacker Namdi Obiazor Round 7, pick 234 : Quarterback Behren Morton Round 7, pick 247 : EDGE Quintayvious Hutchins New England Patriots unofficial depth chart Do not worry about the Patriots not having a punter listed, as Bryce Baringer is on IR and will be back later in the year. Veteran Mitch Wishnowsky will get elevated from the practice squad in his absence. One other note is that pass rusher Harold Landry is starting the year on PUP, so that’s another Super Bowl participant who won’t be factoring into Wednesday’s game. It’d be unwise to assume the rematch will go exactly like the Super Bowl; we already experienced this with the 2014 Seahawks winning an early season overtime thriller over the Broncos after thrashing them in Super Bowl 48. It would, however, be very funny if it does pretty much go the same way despite numerous starting lineup changes.

full_text: Seattle Seahawks' defensive tackle #99 Leonard Williams celebrates on the field after the Seattle Seahawks defeated the New England Patriots during Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California on February 8, 2026. (Photo by JOSH EDELSON / AFP via Getty Images) | AFP via Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks are exactly one week away from their season opener against the New England Patriots. There wasn’t a ton of roster turnover from last year to this year for the Super Bowl champions, but nevertheless we still want to see what the depth chart looks like after a few key names departed in free agency. Without further grandstanding—honestly, I wrote two sentences in the first paragraph, I think I’m getting to this very quickly—here is the Seahawks’ first unofficial depth chart for the 2026 regular season! Seattle Seahawks 2026, Week 1 unofficial depth chart Again, we stress that this is an unofficial depth chart, but the starting lineup for offense and defense looks accurate. There might be some hair-splitting as far as George Holani being listed as RB1 when the expectation is he’ll be sharing carries with Jadarian Price and Emanuel Wilson, but that’s about it on offense. Zach Charbonnet, of course, is not on the depth chart while he awaits his return from the PUP list. Elijah Arroyo is the TE3, but even that could come with the caveat that Seattle’s heavy use of 12 and 13 personnel will see him on the field fairly regularly throughout the season. Bryce Cabeldue played much of camp and preseason as a left guard, so he gets the nod as the backup to Grey Zabel at left guard. Christian Haynes remains the backup right guard to Anthony Bradford, while rookie Beau Stephens is the reserve guard at both positions. Josh Jones is the only backup tackle for either Abe Lucas or Charles Cross. On defense, Derick Hall is not listed as a starter but he functionally is. He was listed as the backup to DeMarcus Lawrence as a “Rush” end last season, so nothing has changed. Meanwhile, Nick Emmanwori is apparently the backup safety for both Ty Okada and Julian Love, but he’s far from a traditional defensive back. It does underscore the point that Seattle’s safety depth on the 53-man roster is scarce. I’m sure Rashid Shaheed and Tory Horton being the primary returners again could create some unease, but keep in mind that George Holani and Montorie Foster are also kick return options.

title: How special teams is reflected in the Seahawks’ initial 53-man roster
summary: When special teams for the Seattle Seahawks is brought up, it’s easy to think names like Rashid Shaheed and Tory Horton. These two delivered some electric and vintage performances on the way to a championship. There were a few. If you’re a ball-knower, Michael Dickson might be your guy. Nick Kallerup, Eric Saubert, and Brady […]
full_text: When special teams for the Seattle Seahawks is brought up, it’s easy to think names like Rashid Shaheed and Tory Horton. These two delivered some electric and vintage performances on the way to a championship . There were a few. If you’re a ball-knower, Michael Dickson might be your guy. Nick Kallerup, Eric Saubert, and Brady Russell also figure to be versatile and tough components of advancing the ball on teams. This team doesn’t play about “the 3rd phase.” HBO’s Hard Knocks director, Pat Harris, called the Seattle Seahawks, “the best in the biz, right now” on The Official Hard Knocks Podcast last week. It is true that we are getting an unprecedented look at the inner workings of an elite sports organization, but the Hawks continue to produce documentary series that shed more and more light on how things tick. The Seattle Seahawks’ media team released a 3-episode installment entitled, “The Specialists.” It documents Jason Myers (he who set a record for most points scored in a single season in NFL history after five Super Bowl FG’s), Rashid Shaheed (Pro Bowl return man) and Michael Dickson (2nd-team, All-Pro punter). Mike Macdonald said of the importance the Seahawks organization places on special teams: “You got to back it up with your actions. So, it’s how you invest in it. It’s who you have out there, it’s who you have coaching them.” In hearing from one of those coaches that is most directly responsible ( Specialists, episode 2 ), we learned what he sees as valuable. Special teams coach, Jay Harbaugh says, “What makes a special teams unit great? You could go on and on and on about that… All the things that would make a defense or an offense great, combined into one. Shaheed, moments later, stated that in 2025, “Special teams was our edge.” Brandon Pili and Connor O’Toole are both on this roster, and they combined for a big turnover in season last year. Harbaugh has not forgotten about the defensive guys in discussing the role of “teams,” which “incorporates both offense and defense, [it’s] interesting to observe different techniques.” As we continue to study who made the 53-man roster, it’s very much worth considering special teams value. The Seahawks certainly do. The Seahawks spend more on their special teams than any other team in the NFL at $9.325M in salary. Their kicker just scored over half the points and their punter downed a punt inside the five-yard-line as Seattle won the Super Bowl. — Front Office Sports (@FOS) February 9, 2026 As far as Mike Macdonald’s defensive scheme goes, in a 3-4 defense, which (presumably) utilizes two off-ball LBs on the field at once, the Hawks kept five. Seattle doesn’t usually rotate that position either. If you play some of the Madden football games, only three will ever really get snaps in a lot of scenarios. This isn’t Madden, but they only kept three on the initial roster last year . Keeping five inside linebackers took away from their ability to keep guys like Jared Ivey (Atlanta), Noah Igbinoghene (Cleveland), Cody White (Las Vegas) and Jamie Sheriff (Los Angeles Rams and their “super team”). That’s an idea worth addressing. Macdonald did discuss finding a role for snaps on defense for Tyrice Knight: “it’s a good problem to have, from a coach’s perspective, of trying to figure out a way to get him out there, and what’s best for the team.” Could he replace a current starter, or is it more likely they find a unique role for him? Emmanwori plays a unique role, but this team likes to have multiple guys who can fill those niche positions. Think D’Anthony Bell backing up E-Man, t times. Think both Leo Williams and “The Polar Bear” (Rylie Mills, a nickname revealed to us by “Big Cat” during one of the preseason games) lining up at DT, but also EDGE at times. Think of both Mike Morris, as well as Jared Ivey playing big-bodied ends, but moonlighting on the interior of the defensive line at times. Think both Knight and Drake Thomas taking snaps on the outside edge of the defense. Shaheed, a former UDFA who made the Saints’ roster, went on later, in his episode of “The Specialists,” to state plainly: “It’s not everybody’s dream to be on special teams, but it’s always a dream to play in the NFL.” Whether a new LB role (that pulls in Knight, as well as other candidates) emerges or not, Morris, Patrick O’Connell and Chazz Surratt will be invaluable members of the Seattle Seahawks special teams squads as defensive guys. The linebackers, in particular might offer unique instincts, football intelligence, and physicality. That could be the biggest reason that it seems Seattle loaded up at that position. I mean, go back up top and click on the hyperlink “electric”, and you’ll see Surratt throw a key block on Horton’s punt return TD against the Saints. Side note : it may not be the first thing that comes to mind, even on special teams, but I hope there is an episode that gets added later, covering long snapper, Chris Stoll. After the Super Bowl win, Mike Dicko, the kicker said : “Oh yeah, Stoley… he’s the best in the world. He — some of the snaps today just felt like a video game. They came out so perfectly”. He went on to talk about the difficulty of his task, saying, “to be upside-down and be able to throw a ball backwards through the air to a spot this big brings his hands together to form a circle .” These special teamers deserve more of our respect for what they do outside of the limelight.

title: 49ers pass rush takes another hit as starter listed as questionable with a foot injury
summary: Late Wednesday night, multiple San Francisco 49ers reporters said Sam Okuayinonu is not flying with the team to Australia because of a foot injury. Okuayinonu will have a questionable designation for Week 1. It’s not out of the question that he travels later on and can still play, but it’s not a good sign he […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 17: Sam Okuayinonu #91 of the San Francisco 49ers reacts after making a tackle during the second quarter of an NFL divisional playoff football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on January 17, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Late Wednesday night, multiple San Francisco 49ers reporters said Sam Okuayinonu is not flying with the team to Australia because of a foot injury. Okuayinonu will have a questionable designation for Week 1. It’s not out of the question that he travels later on and can still play, but it’s not a good sign he isn’t traveling with everybody else. According to NBC Sports Bay Area’s Matt Maiocco, everybody else traveled. The 49ers are already paper-thin when it comes to the health of their edge rushers. Nick Bosa did team drills for the first time during Wednesday’s practice . Bosa practicing is a great sign. However, it’s unlikely he’ll be able to work his way into football shape in a week. Bosa and Okuyinonu were likely the first two defensive ends to take the field. They are the two best, and arguably only, run-stopping options at the position. Keion White is better suited inside, while Romello Height — who made plays and was competitive against the run in the preseason — was drafted to rush the passer. The 49ers were likely to elevate Ogbo Okoronkwo from the practice squad before Okuayinonu’s injury. That’s inevitable now if Sam O can’t suit up. There might need to be another move at the position if Romello Height continues to miss practice with an ankle injury. In an ideal world, Sam O plays on early downs, with White and Height spelling him on passing downs. But without Okuayinonu, and potentially Height, White has to rush predominantly from the edge since you’re short on bodies. In contrast, defensive tackles Alfred Collins and CJ West may have to pick up the slack on passing downs. We could find out how much Morris trusts rookie Jaden Dugger earlier than expected. Injuries could force his hand into more 5-man fronts with Dugger walked down on the line of scrimmage. That may have been the case, regardless of Okuayinonu or Height’s availability, given how many three-tight-end sets the Rams use. The domino effect of potential injuries up front will test Raheem Morris’s creativity and the Niners’ depth.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers News: We are officially one week away from real football
summary: 49ers’ Nick Bosa practices fully for first time since ACL injury“Bosa’s recovery from the knee injury hasn’t been linear. He was far enough along in his rehab that he didn’t need to start the preseason on the physically unable to perform list and was doing individual drills on the side during the opening days of […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - DECEMBER 12: Nick Bosa #97 of the San Francisco 49ers pressures Matthew Stafford #9 of the Los Angeles Rams during the game at Levi's Stadium on December 12, 2024 in Santa Clara, California. The Rams defeated the 49ers 12-6. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images 49ers’ Nick Bosa practices fully for first time since ACL injury “Bosa’s recovery from the knee injury hasn’t been linear. He was far enough along in his rehab that he didn’t need to start the preseason on the physically unable to perform list and was doing individual drills on the side during the opening days of training camp in July. But Bosa had a setback that the team originally described as soreness and then later added that he was dealing with knee tendinitis. On Wednesday, Bosa offered a deeper look into the series of fits and starts he has dealt with in his comeback. “It was a long road,” Bosa said. “There’s some stuff I dealt with, with that patella tendon, and then I kind of ramped it a little too fast with the football stuff a month ago or whatever it was. And that kind of told me to back off. I’ve just been trying to get it as strong and myself as confident as I can to where I could rip the Band-Aid off and go to team stuff today.” ….The next challenge for Bosa will be to make it through the 16-hour flight the team is set to take to Melbourne on Wednesday night. Bosa said he plans to use the “Game Ready” machine, which is a sleeve for his legs that combines compression and ice at the same time, a few times; ice his knees; use a foam roller; and stretch as well as making sure he gets enough sleep. From there, Bosa said the next step to returning to play will be participating in the four practices (Saturday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday) the team has scheduled in Australia. The NFL will require the Niners to have an official injury report for the first time this season after Monday’s practice.” Grading the 49ers’ initial 53-man roster: Is this a Super Bowl-caliber team? “Guess who makes the offensive line better? Mike Evans. The blocking shouldn’t be as congested as it was a season ago with a legitimate WR1 who can win outside of the numbers. Quantifying offensive linemen on a down-to-down basis is one of the most difficult things to do in football. They could do their jobs to perfection, but if the quarterback doesn’t get rid of the ball in time, or the running back doesn’t go where he’s supposed to, the line gets assigned the blame. For the longest time, Kyle Shanahan’s offensive lines have been known as the sum being greater than the parts. Despite constant fan blame, I thought the line turned a corner last season. With a better supporting cast, this group will be viewed much more positively this season. Because no one dominates besides Williams, individual matchups are the one area where the line can be susceptible. I mean something along the lines of Myles Garrett versus Colton McKivitz, or Josh Sweat against Carver Willis — the extreme mismatches. As a unit, there are few busted assignments….At their best, Green and Lenoir look like a high-end CB2. In fairness, that’s been without a semblance of a pass rush. The Niners are hoping that changes this season. You still have to cover on third down, and that was an issue last season, even when the quarterback didn’t have five seconds to throw. This group’s variance makes them the most unpredictable on the team. We need to see better coverage skills from Upton Stout in Year 2. And if Morris is going to run more man-to-man concepts, the perimeter cornerbacks will need to do a better job of holding their own.” Kawakami: John Lynch on the 49ers’ goals heading to Australia and beyond (paywall) “For years there were teams that wouldn’t touch guys that were a little bit older, 24, 25,” Lynch said. “I think by virtue of NIL and all that, that’s the reality of this league now. But I think maybe we’re seeing some of the advantages. They’ve got some pelts on the wall, they’ve been through a variety of situations. They’ve transferred different places — all three of them, on multiple occasions. And that used to mean, like, what’s wrong with this guy? Why is he transferring? Now it’s just part of the landscape that we’re forced to deal with. … “Something I keep thinking of is that [Stribling, Height, and Enrique Cruz Jr.], they’re all sons of marines. I think you see it in their discipline. You know, we knew that about each of them. We didn’t say, ‘We’re only drafting sons of marines,’ but it’s pretty cool to see the impact of that, because you can tell they’ve taken hard coaching, probably at their home, and they aren’t averse to that. There’s a little more maturity by virtue of their age, by virtue of the circumstances they’ve dealt with, with transferring, and there’s some added value there. I think that has them ready to embrace this moment, and we’ll see how they take advantage of the opportunity.”….“Kyle’s a wonderful person; he’s fun, he’s funny; but he challenges everything. And sometimes will get a little ornery,” Lynch said with a chuckle. “And I think some of that in the last 15 days, you know, some of that [has been] coming out. And challenging things. … “And then, ultimately, just talk to [his wife] Mandy. Mandy will tell you where he’s at. She said, ‘Alright, he’s good.’ And I believe that.” 49ers star Nick Bosa shares encouraging update about Week 1 status vs. Rams “I’ve gotten a good amount of cardio work and I feel explosive,” he said. “But once I throw pads on, that’s another aspect of it that I’ll get this week. But I think the wind comes pretty quick for me. Once I get out there, once I get through the first drive, it just gets fun.” Inside Brock Purdy’s ever-evolving leadership role as 49ers’ star quarterback “When I first got into the league, it was all about, for me, learning the offense, learning myself, how I can get better and always accepting the coaching,” he said. “I still do that, but now I’m at a point where these young guys and the new guys that come in, I want to get them on track as fast as I can with the standard that we play at, the standard that they need to be playing at for our offense to move as a machine.” Purdy, 26, showed those leadership qualities on the practice field during training camp. It was not uncommon to see him exhorting his teammates to execute at high levels and not repeat mental mistakes…. “The biggest thing for me is building trust,” Purdy said. “When we’re out on the field and we’re under all that heat and pressure of executing and winning games, what it comes down to is trust. “Can I trust you? Can you trust me to make the right decisions in the heat of the moment and do it over and over again, over a long stretch of a long season…If there’s a moment where I can call a guy out, it’s because I trust him and I love him and I want him to understand what it means to me, and vice versa,” Purdy said. “But I think there’s definitely a way to go about it. And at the end of the day, I think my teammates know that. They love it. I love being able to be honest with them, and they know that it comes from an authentic place in my heart.” 49ers stars return to practice on Wednesday before team’s flight to Australia “Evans and Juszczyk made their returns to the practice field, too. Evans has been dealing with a tight groin, while Juszczyk has been out since Aug. 5 with a fractured finger.”
author: Yinon Raviv

title: 49ers injury updates: Nick Bosa opens up about his recovery; 2 rookies still out
summary: The San Francisco 49ers had one final practice before they head to Australia. Several starters returning from injury took part in Wednesday’s session: Nick Bosa (ACL)George Kittle (Achilles)Kyle Juszczyk (broken finger)Mike Evans (adductor) Those are objectively among the best and most important players on the roster. According to Tim Kawakami, Bosa and Kittle will fly […]
full_text: San Francisco 49ers defensive end Nick Bosa (97) during training at the Levi's Stadium practice field in Santa Clara on Sunday, July 26, 2026. (Photo by Santiago Mejia/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images) The San Francisco 49ers had one final practice before they head to Australia. Several starters returning from injury took part in Wednesday’s session: Nick Bosa (ACL) George Kittle (Achilles) Kyle Juszczyk (broken finger) Mike Evans (adductor) Those are objectively among the best and most important players on the roster. According to Tim Kawakami , Bosa and Kittle will fly to Australia. That’s a step in the right direction. Bosa spoke with the media after practice and said he felt great during practice. Bosa went as far as to say he’s confident he’ll play Week 1, as long as he continues on his current path. He also spoke about ramping up too quickly: “I’m not going to go back too far because every recovery there’s ups and downs, but it was a long road. There’s some stuff I dealt with, with that patella tendon, and then I kind of ramped it a little too fast with the football stuff a month ago or whatever it was. And that kind of told me to back off. I’ve just been trying to get it as strong and myself as confident as I can to where I could rip the bandaid off and go to team stuff today. Because once you get into team, there’s no reservations, there’s no compensation, like there’s no governor. So yeah, I felt that today. I remember my last ACL, there was a couple moments where you just have to go and you’re kind of hoping for the best. Obviously it’s not going to be like anything crazy is going to happen, but you hope that your body is going to respond the way that you prepared it to. And there’s a couple moments today where that happened. So I’m just going to try and keep building, not get too up about it, but it was a great day.” The top 1% of the 1% have performance anxiety. It makes you appreciate Bosa being transparent about the mental hurdle he’s been dealing with. Raheem Morris said high-end athletes are in tune with their bodies better than anyone. If you’re Morris, you unleash Bosa if he’s healthy and let him be the one to tell you when he needs a breather. Here are a couple of clips of Bosa from the reporters on the scene: 49ers practice log 🏈 Back in warmups DL Bosa (support sleeve on knee) WR Evans FB Juszczyk CB Prysock Side field training: DL Height, Halton WR Cowing CB Green LB Gifford pic.twitter.com/QQsGY9sX3j — Cam Inman (@CamInman) September 2, 2026 Nick Bosa is back. pic.twitter.com/uiIN4Ebpie — Harrison Rich (@harrisonrich_) September 2, 2026 At first glance, Bosa looked leaner. I’d be interested to know if shed any weight during the past calendar year. Regardless, Bosa practicing and traveling is what you want to hear a week away from the first game. Here’s a list of the players who did not participate on Wednesday: CB Renardo Green ( hamstring ) WR Jacob Cowing ( groin ) LB Luke Gifford (hamstring) DT Gracen Halton (ankle) DE Romello Height ( ankle ) DT James Thompson Jr. (undisclosed) Green’s hamstring injury has been lingering since the end of July. Green has the body type you want to go against Puka Nacua (if he plays), Davante Adams, and the three Rams tight ends that stand 6’5″, 6’6″, and 6’7″. Green’s backup, Jack Jones, came into the NFL weighing in at the first percentile among cornerbacks. Unfortunately, Jones didn’t do any work with the team. Multiple reporters tweeted that Jones was working on the side of the field. There’s no word on what Jones’ injury was. More than likely, he tweaked something. We’ll provide updates once they are available. The 49ers are a Green-and-Jones injury away from starting the regular season with a Day 3 rookie corner playing his first game in a brand-new environment against the best offense in the NFL. Gulp. Staying with the rookies, Halton’s injury occurred before the second preseason game. Height’s ankle was hurt ahead of the third preseason game. It’s been multiple weeks since both players practiced. At this point, it’d be surprising if we saw them in Week 1.
author: Kyle Posey

title: What are the biggest concerns heading into Week 1 for the 49ers?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are wrapping up their final practice session before boarding a flight to Australia ahead of the season opener on September 10th, or the 11th if you’re in Australia. Eight days is an eternity in 49ers land, but as of now, things are looking positive for the team before they clash with […]
full_text: The San Francisco 49ers are wrapping up their final practice session before boarding a flight to Australia ahead of the season opener on September 10th, or the 11th if you’re in Australia. Eight days is an eternity in 49ers land, but as of now, things are looking positive for the team before they clash with the Los Angeles Rams. Aside from the second meeting between the division rivals in 2025, every game comes down to the wire or down to a few plays to decide the winner. You can expect that trend to continue. Here are the biggest concerns for the 49ers heading into Week 1: Nick Bosa, Mike Evans and George Kittle’s health The good news is both players were practicing today and are flying to Australia, according to reports. It should be viewed as a good sign that both would travel. If either player were in danger of missing Week 1, they wouldn’t fly and put their body through the long flight. Both Bosa and Kittle are vital to the 49ers’ success, but without a fully healthy, effective Bosa, the 49ers’ defense takes a huge hit. The goal is to get both through the season, but today is a positive step for both playing in Australia. Mike Evans also returned, which is a welcome sight, and his presence and production are needed for the 2026 49ers offense. Managing all three will be key for the 49ers. The left guard spot When Kyle Shanahan says they haven’t decided who will start at left guard and brought in veteran IOL Jarett Patterson via trade with the Houston Texans, it doesn’t evoke a ton of confidence. The team has been looking for a consistent starter since Aaron Banks’s departure. The problem is that neither Carver Willis nor Connor Colby has taken a definitive lead in the race to start. Both have good plays on tape, but the consistency is a concern. Is the answer as simple as turning to Patterson? That remains to be seen, but this many options can’t be viewed as a good thing. The decision looms large. Who will start opposite Deommodore Lenoir in Week 1? Renardo Green is dealing with a hamstring injury, but today’s practice report added veteran cornerback Jack Jones working off on the side field and working through an undisclosed injury at the moment. With Green not practicing and the flight to Australia today, coupled with a banged-up Jones. The question of the second outside cornerback becomes much more of a concern with the team facing Davante Adams and Puka Nacua, potentially. It’s easy to name the safety position, but Ephesians Prysock could get a welcome-to-the-NFL moment if Green and Jones are out for Week 1.
author: Jason Aponte

title: Can De’Zhaun Stribling break any 49ers’ rookie records this year?
summary: Rookie wide receivers haven’t exactly prospered with the San Francisco 49ers under head coach Kyle Shanahan. They can’t seem to escape the proverbial doghouse. Brandon Aiyuk (60) and Deebo Samuel (57) were the only players to surpass 35 receptions. Unsurprisingly, that pair was also the only duo to have at least 500 yards receiving during […]
full_text: EL SEGUNDO, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 18: De'Zhaun Stribling #15 of the San Francisco 49ers makes a reception during the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Chargers Joint Practice at The Bolt on August 18, 2026 in El Segundo, California. (Photo by Kevin Terrell/Getty Images) | Getty Images Rookie wide receivers haven’t exactly prospered with the San Francisco 49ers under head coach Kyle Shanahan. They can’t seem to escape the proverbial doghouse. Brandon Aiyuk (60) and Deebo Samuel (57) were the only players to surpass 35 receptions. Unsurprisingly, that pair was also the only duo to have at least 500 yards receiving during their rookie seasons. Ricky Pearsall’s rookie year has a giant asterisk . He came on strong in the second half with 31 receptions for 400 yards. Six seasons before that, Dante Pettis caught 27 passes for 467 yards. Close, but no cigar. Jauan Jennings didn’t play in 2020, so he was still technically a rookie in 2021. Jennings caught 24 passes for 282 yards. Jennings is actually tied for second all-time in franchise history with five receiving touchdowns (Jennings and Aiyuk also had 5) during his rookie campaign. ESPN’s Dan Graziano went through each team, saying, “Don’t be surprised if.” For the 49ers, it was about De’Zhaun Stribling: Don’t be surprised if … De’Zhaun Stribling leads all rookie wide receivers in catches. What I’m hearing: Yes, free agent signee Mike Evans is likely to be the team’s top wide receiver (but he’s already dealing with injuries in training camp). Yes, veterans Demarcus Robinson and Deebo Samuel Sr . have put in more time with this coaching staff and in this system. And yes, Kyle Shanahan’s history tells us he’s reluctant to put too much faith in rookie receivers. But all of that said, someone needs to catch the ball in San Francisco, and Stribling has been doing a lot of that in camp and the preseason. The first pick of the second round of this year’s draft, Stribling has a chance to make an impact as a rookie. Left tackle Trent Williams told me he expects big things from Stribling right away — that he reminds him of former 49ers receiver Jauan Jennings in terms of the variety of routes he can run but with more speed. Brock Purdy could look Stribling’s way early and often, and he could be a high-volume pass catcher. The 49ers didn’t draft Stribling to ease him into the lineup. He’s going to play early and often. He brings a different element than Robinson and Deebo — who are role players, at best, at this point in their careers. Stribling looked like a budding star in the preseason. He should have plenty of opportunities to rack up numbers as a rookie. He may not have the seasons Aiyuk and Deebo did, since so many other options are on the roster. But at the same time, his floor could be what a couple of rookies did back in the ‘90s—looking at a J.J. Stokes/Terrell Owens rookie year. Those two had just over 500 receiving yards and 35 and 38 receptions, respectively. Since 2021, 11 receivers have surpassed 1,000 yards. Another five have had 900-yard seasons as rookies. My prediction is somewhere along the lines of what George Pickens did with the Steelers in 2022: 52 receptions for 801 yards and four touchdowns. To ESPN’s point, that might be enough to lead all receivers.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Richard Sherman on 49ers IOL approach: ‘I don’t really get it’
summary: The San Francisco 49ers didn’t make many major changes to the offensive line this offseason, running it back with starters Trent Williams, Jake Brendel, Dominick Puni, and Colton McKivitz. They elected not to spend much capital in both free agency and the draft on the position. They signed Vederian Lowe to a two-year, $9.25 million […]
full_text: Oct 19, 2025; Santa Clara, California, USA; San Francisco 49ers guard Connor Colby (75) before the game against the Atlanta Falcons at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The San Francisco 49ers didn’t make many major changes to the offensive line this offseason, running it back with starters Trent Williams, Jake Brendel, Dominick Puni, and Colton McKivitz. They elected not to spend much capital in both free agency and the draft on the position. They signed Vederian Lowe to a two-year, $9.25 million deal to be their swing tackle. Brett Toth got a one-year, $2.5 million deal to compete at guard. And Robert Jones was the only other main free agency addition, signing a one-year, $1.75 million deal to also compete at left guard with Connor Colby. The 49ers also waited for Day 3 of the draft to address the position, drafting Washington offensive lineman Carver Willis in the fourth round and Kansas offensive tackle Enrique Cruz Jr. in the fifth round. That set up a competition at left guard this offseason, and it’s mainly been process of elimination, with Willis being the candidate progressing the most through training camp. Still, the results from all candidates have been quite mixed this offseason, with injuries also getting in the way. So, the 49ers ended up trading a Day 3 pick for Houston Texans offensive lineman Jarrett Patterson on cutdown day, and he’s expected to immediately get reps at center and guard, with Kyle Shanahan also saying the starting left guard hasn’t been decided yet. Over the years, analysts have criticized the 49ers for their approach towards the offensive line. They haven’t spent a first-round pick at the position since Mike McGlinchey in 2018, and haven’t also made many significant free agent investments outside of re-signing players. Following the Patterson trade, former 49ers cornerback Richard Sherman gave his thoughts on the offensive line, sharing his concerns with the team’s approach. “The thing they didn’t do that I was concerned about was that interior offensive line. They didn’t strengthen it,” Sherman said. “Now, we’re late into training camp. Training camp is done. We’re late in the offseason. We’re a week away from the season, and they’re trading for interior offensive linemen because it’s an obvious place of concern. We knew that two years ago. And that’s the part where I don’t really get it. “You’re about to go against the most dynamic D-Lines in the league in LA and Seattle. Two of the most incredible D-Lines in the league, and you’re just gonna say, hey, we’ll figure it out as we go. Against Aaron Donald? Against Leonard Williams, Byron Murphy, Jarran Reed? That’s what you’re gonna go with? That’s the plan? That’s the part with the San Francisco 49ers where I’m like, the roster building, I don’t understand it.” The 49ers have invested a couple of higher draft picks at the position in the Kyle Shanahan era. They took McGlinchey in 2018 in the first round. They took Aaron Banks in the second round of the 2021 NFL Draft. But in 10 drafts, those are the only two top-two-round picks that the 49ers have spent on the offensive line. Here’s who they’ve drafted in the last five years: 2022: Spencer Burford (fourth round), Nick Zakelj (sixth round) 2023: N/A 2024: Dominick Puni (third round), Jarrett Kingston (sixth round) 2025: Connor Colby (seventh round) 2026: Carver Willis (fourth round), Enrique Cruz (fifth round) Of that group, there’s really only one hit, and that’s Dominick Puni. That’s not ideal. Going back even further across all the 10 years of drafts under Shanahan and John Lynch, the 49ers have taken Aaron Banks (second round), Jaylon Moore (fifth round), Colton McKivitz (fifth round), Justin Skule (sixth round), and Mike McGlinchey (first round). Of that group, McKivitz is the only true steal, and that came after he was initially cut by the team. Banks is the only other “hit” and he’s been average at best throughout his NFL career, while not earning a second contract with the 49ers. Same goes for McGlinchey, who probably hasn’t lived up to his No. 9 overall draft slot while being a serviceable right tackle. Not only are the 49ers not drafting in quantity, but they haven’t invested much capital into the position group as a whole. We’ll see if it ends up hurting them this year, but they’re currently still figuring out a starter at left guard this close to the season.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: George Kittle ‘trending in the right direction’ for Week 1
summary: The 49ers’ season opener will be nearly exactly months on from George Kittle tearing his Achilles in their wild-card round win over the Philadelphia Eagles. It appears he will mark the occasion by making his return to the field. Kittle’s status has been one of the big questions hanging over the 49ers ahead of their […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 11: George Kittle #85 of the San Francisco 49ers lines up before the snap during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 11, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 49ers’ season opener will be nearly exactly months on from George Kittle tearing his Achilles in their wild-card round win over the Philadelphia Eagles. It appears he will mark the occasion by making his return to the field. Kittle’s status has been one of the big questions hanging over the 49ers ahead of their 2026 season opener against the Los Angeles Rams in Melbourne, Australia. But the star tight end will make the 15-hour journey on Wednesday as the 49ers head Down Under a week early to acclimate to the time difference, with the signs seemingly pointing to him playing at the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground. NFL Network and ESPN’s Ian Rapoport reported early on Wednesday that Kittle has had two positive days of practice and is “trending in the right direction to play”. That would obviously be a massive boost to the 49er offense with everything Kittle brings as both a pass-catcher and as a blocker in the run game. The drop-off in the latter area when he is not on the field has long since been apparent. There is still concern from a defensive perspective concerning Nick Bosa, though Rapoport reported Bosa is “ramping up” his knee as he deals with tendinitis/soreness connected to his ACL reconstruction. Bosa will also make the trip and, for as key as Kittle is the offense, it is arguably more important for the 49ers’ hopes of beating the Rams that the former Defensive Player of the Year is able to get on the field. San Francisco is extremely thin at defensive end. Simply put, they do not have any fearsome outside pass rushers beyond Bosa, and their prospects of generating a pass rush that can help slow down Matthew Stafford and Co. will diminish dramatically if he is not able to play. With Kittle out there, the 49ers have a better chance of keeping up with the Rams in a potential shootout, but they desperately need Bosa to be ready to get the stops they will need to ensure this most arduous of road trips ends in celebration.
author: Nicholas McGee

title: Grading the 49ers’ initial 53-man roster: Is this a Super Bowl-caliber team?
summary: Now that we’ve had a day or so to process the San Francisco 49ers’ initial 53-man roster and digest the moves that were made, it’s time to evaluate how deep this roster is. Is this a one-and-done playoff team? Can they win the division? Or are we talking about a deep playoff run? Let’s grade the current […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 20: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers throws a pass against the Los Angeles Chargers during the first quarter in a preseason game at SoFi Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images Now that we’ve had a day or so to process the San Francisco 49ers’ initial 53-man roster and digest the moves that were made, it’s time to evaluate how deep this roster is. Is this a one-and-done playoff team? Can they win the division? Or are we talking about a deep playoff run? Let’s grade the current iteration of the 49ers. Quarterbacks (3) Starter: Brock Purdy Backups: Mac Jones, Kurtis Rourke This is the best quarterback room the 49ers have had under Kyle Shanahan. Brock Purdy is the best starter. Mac Jones is the best backup (it was a different Sam Darnold then). And Kurtis Rourke is rookie-year Purdy. The team knowing Rourke wasn’t worth losing on waivers shows foresight into what he means to this team down the line. My not-so-bold prediction is that Purdy plays every game and has a career year. He’ll be playing with the best supporting cast of his life. The wide receivers give Purdy more margin for error than he’s ever had. Plus, quietly, it’s legs should win at least a series-a-game for the offense. Maybe it’s something as simple as escaping a sack and living to fight another down. It very well could mean scrambling for a first down when nothing is there. But I believe the QB tiers from this past offseason will look foolish by season’s end. Grade: A Running backs (4) Starters: Christian McCaffrey, Kyle Juszczyk Backups: Kaelon Black, Jordan James Another strong group for the Niners. Less might be more with Christian McCaffrey early on in the season as the team preserves him for a second-half run. I don’t see a point in giving McCaffrey 30 touches a game in September and October — especially when there are viable options behind him. Reminiscent of 2023, not the version of McCaffrey, but the depth of the running back room. Elijah Mitchell had 75 carries that season. Jordan James had 40 and averaged 5.2 yards per carry. If Kaelon Black and Jordan James can assume that kind of volume, the running game will be potent. Both backups ran well in the preseason. They were decisive, and it led to first downs. Each one of them being able to contribute in the passing game, whether it’s in pass protection or as a receiver, makes it a complete unit. Black and James’ youth will mean inevitable mistakes, but it’s something they’ll need to play through. Grade: A- Wide receivers (6) Starters: Mike Evans, De’Zhaun Stribling, Deebo Samuel, Demarcus Robinson Backups: Jordan Watkins, Jacob Cowing The 49ers are expecting Mike Evans back at practice next week as he deals with an adductor injury. The reason it’s easy to be optimistic in the ground game is that safeties can’t hover around the line of scrimmage knowing Evans is lurking on the perimeter. Another reason to be optimistic about the rushing attack is that Evans and Stribling are now the primary blockers. Aaron Donald is objectively one of the best defensive players of this generation. He has not played since 2023. He is 35. Yet, you’d think he’s coming off an All-Pro season the way he’s being discussed. Evans is objectively one of the best wide receivers of this generation. He’s a season removed from missing eight games. Evans is 33. For the previous nine years, 1,000-yard seasons were the norm. Brock is going to have his best season because of Evans. The rushing attack will be at its best because of Evans. Every other receiver on the roster will reap the rewards of Evans. Is there a worry that he’ll miss time? Of course. But with the 49ers’ maintenance plan of not having Evans practice three days in a row, that should aid in keeping Evans available for game days. Stribling gives Purdy his first contested-catch receiver, aside from Evans. While you may think Jauan Jennings was in a similar mode, he was below 50% last season in contested situations. Stribling’s speed was already on full display in the preseason. Deebo will be a jack-of-all-trades. I expect him to live underneath for free access yards. He might be at his best coming out of the backfield as a pass catcher. I saw the results of Evans firsthand and how Robinson got open because of it. I suspect he’ll be Cowing will be the wild card. Best case, Cowing ends up in a Travis Benjamin-esque role from when Shanahan was with the Browns a decade ago. Cowing won’t be a 1,000-yard receiver, but the splash plays will keep the defense honest and the running back will be the beneficiary. Evans is carrying this grade. We live in a world of, “what have you done for me lately?” We forget who Evans is, the situation he’s in, and how athletes generally bounce back and go on a tear when they believe everyone doubts them. Grade: B+ Tight ends (4) Starter: George Kittle Backups: Luke Farrell, Jake Tonges, Brayden Willis Willis making the roster felt like a hedge in case Kittle can’t play right away. Still, keeping a seventh-rounder who has been on and off the roster felt like a risk you didn’t need to take. That’s not to take away from what Willis did in the preseason, but it felt like he would’ve cleared waivers. It’ll be fascinating to see Kittle’s usage coming off an Achilles injury. We know blocking won’t be an issue. But will he be used down the field? Will it matter? Against the Rams linebackers, probably not. Kittle will be 1-on-1 in almost every scenario this season — another way the offense will enjoy the fruits of Evans. It’ll still be a wait-and-see with Farrell. Players tend to improve in Year 2 of Shanahan’s offense. In Farrell’s case, there’s only one direction to go. Tonges is closer to good than average as a receiver, but it’s clear the team doesn’t want him to block. Ideally, we see Tonges more as a receiver, but I’m not holding my breath. Kittle turns 33 in August and is coming off another serious injury. As much as I’d like to give an all-world player the benefit of the doubt, I have to be realistic with him and this group’s expectations. Grade: C+ Offensive line (9) Starters: Trent Williams, Carver Willis**, Jake Brendel, Dominick Puni, Colton McKivitz Backups: Vederian Lowe, Enrique Cruz, Connor Colby, Jarrett Patterson The rookie Willis gets the nod, unless Patterson comes in and steals the show. According to Brandon Thorn’s almanac , the 49ers have the sixth-most experienced unit, with the 11th-most talented. They’re on the older side, ranking 24th—which is saying something, considering a rookie and a third-year pro are starting. He had a fun nugget: The 49ers’ projected line is 33 combined years older than the Dolphins’, while the tackles are the third-lightest starting duo in the league. Willis aside, the continuity is where you want it. We’ll find out if the production follows. Guess who makes the offensive line better? Mike Evans. The blocking shouldn’t be as congested as it was a season ago with a legitimate WR1 who can win outside of the numbers. Quantifying offensive linemen on a down-to-down basis is one of the most difficult things to do in football. They could do their jobs to perfection, but if the quarterback doesn’t get rid of the ball in time, or the running back doesn’t go where he’s supposed to, the line gets assigned the blame. For the longest time, Kyle Shanahan’s offensive lines have been known as the sum being greater than the parts. Despite constant fan blame, I thought the line turned a corner last season. With a better supporting cast, this group will be viewed much more positively this season. Because no one dominates besides Williams, individual matchups are the one area where the line can be susceptible. I mean something along the lines of Myles Garrett versus Colton McKivitz, or Josh Sweat against Carver Willis — the extreme mismatches. As a unit, there are few busted assignments.
