title: Will CB Melvin Smith add something to Titans, or is he just another Jalyn Armour-Davis?
summary: The Tennessee Titans were awarded three players off waivers on Monday. Among the new additions was cornerback Melvin Smith. The Titans also signed safety Terrell Burgess and offensive tackle James Hudson, making five total additions after the initial 53-man roster was set. Smith entered the league as an undrafted free agent with the Kansas City […]
full_text: Aug 9, 2025; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Kansas City Chiefs cornerback Melvin Smith Jr. (39) against the Arizona Cardinals during a preseason NFL game at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Tennessee Titans were awarded three players off waivers on Monday. Among the new additions was cornerback Melvin Smith. The Titans also signed safety Terrell Burgess and offensive tackle James Hudson , making five total additions after the initial 53-man roster was set. Smith entered the league as an undrafted free agent with the Kansas City Chiefs last offseason. Titans GM Mike Borgonzi was already in Tennessee, meaning he isn’t directly connected to Smith through his KC days. It’s safe to assume the tendencies he searches for in late-round cornerbacks is still in place with the Chiefs, however. Smith played 47 total snaps for the Chiefs during this recent preseason period. The former Southern Arkansas standout allowed four receptions for 29 yards and a touchdown, per Pro Football Focus. He also had six tackles. The Titans waived Erick Hallett II to make room for Smith on the 53-man roster. It was a bit surprising, because Hallett played pretty well throughout training camp and the preseason. He has since been re-signed to the practice squad, so at least Borgonzi managed to retain him. Smith did not play a single regular-season snap for the Chiefs in 2025. He essentially spent his entire rookie campaign on the practice squad. The Chiefs brought in multiple new cornerbacks this offseason, including former Titans L’Jarius Sneed and Kristian Fulton. They also drafted multiple corners, including first-round pick Mansoor Delane. That made Smith expendable to them. It’s worth remembering the Titans claimed two cornerbacks off waivers last season. They added Jalyn Armour-Davis and Sam Womack II via the wire process. Armour-Davis was a downright liability, and Womack couldn’t really get on the field for them. Most waiver additions amount to nothing; that’s why they’re available in late August. Borgonzi’s history with late-round cornerbacks in Kansas City makes the Smith addition interesting. Together, they found gems like Joshua Williams, Sneed, and Jaylen Watson. Speaking of Williams, he begins his first season with the Titans on short-term IR. That makes Smith the fifth cornerback right now. Hopefully Smith turns into a waiver-wire gem.

title: Did the Titans get better by replacing Austin Deculus with James Hudson?
summary: After initially making four roster moves on Monday, one obvious to-do item remained for the Tennessee Titans. They claimed Owen Pappoe (LB), Melvin Smith (CB), and Nazir Stackhouse (DT) off waivers, and signed veteran safety Terrell Burgess. To make room, they waived Mo Diabate (LB), Erick Hallett II (CB), Jerrick Reed II (SS), and Xavier […]
full_text: Aug 22, 2021; Cleveland, Ohio, USA; Cleveland Browns offensive tackle James Hudson (66) blocks against the New York Giants during the second quarter at FirstEnergy Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Scott Galvin-USA TODAY Sports After initially making four roster moves on Monday, one obvious to-do item remained for the Tennessee Titans . They claimed Owen Pappoe (LB), Melvin Smith (CB), and Nazir Stackhouse (DT) off waivers, and signed veteran safety Terrell Burgess. To make room, they waived Mo Diabate (LB), Erick Hallett II (CB), Jerrick Reed II (SS), and Xavier Restrepo (WR). Fans quickly noted the lack of a swing tackle, which everyone believed would be Mike Borgonzi’s biggest priority. The other shoe eventually dropped. Making a fifth move, the Titans signed offensive tackle James Hudson and waived Austin Deculus. Deculus struggled mightily throughout the preseason, allowing three sacks to backups. He was passed over on the depth chart by sophomore UDFA Brandon Crenshaw-Dickson. Now, Deculus is off the roster altogether, making room for Hudson. Hudson previously played for Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll with the New York Giants . His position coach was Titans OL coach Carmen Bricillo. He was even teammates with new starting center Austin Schlottmann. At least Hudson will be familiar with the scheme. Hudson played just 85 offensive snaps last season. He last played meaningful snaps in 2024, earning 207 reps at left tackle. Hudson wasn’t credited with allowing any sacks, but he did give up 15 pressures while earning a pass-blocking grade of 40.2 (PFF). The sample size was significantly larger in 2023, earning 493 snaps at right tackle. The former fourth-round selection out of Cincinnati forfeited five sacks and 36 pressures en route to a pass-blocking score of 48.4. He’s known as a powerful run blocker, but his pass-blocking grades have been better than Deculus’ (33.1 in 2025). Hudson represents an upgrade from Deculus, but the Titans’ offense could still be troublesome if he had to play meaningful snaps. At least Hudson has played both tackle positions, and knows Daboll/Bricillo from his past. The Titans still have a long-term problem, but at least he’s better than Deculus.

full_text: The Washington Commanders were in Ashburn today for the last practice of the week and also the first padded practice of the regular season. Odafe Oweh (calf) will be back at practice next week, but Quinn wouldn’t commit to him being available for Week 1 until he sees his return on the field. Quinn said leadership is critical at the linebacker position, and Styles has shown that throughout the offseason and training camp/preseason. title: How Stefon Diggs ‘fire’ has helped improve Washington Commanders
summary: The Commanders needed a solid No. 2 receiver entering training camp to fortify the position group and make it complete. That was clear and evident early on, with an experienced veteran opposite Terry McLaurin who could allow rookie Antonio Williams to develop at a proper place.   Washington was patient in the marketplace but maintained […]
full_text: The Commanders needed a solid No. 2 receiver entering training camp to fortify the position group and make it complete. That was clear and evident early on, with an experienced veteran opposite Terry McLaurin who could allow rookie Antonio Williams to develop at a proper place. Washington was patient in the marketplace but maintained a presence there, eventually agreeing to terms on a one-year deal with DMV native and University of Maryland product Stefon Diggs. The veteran’s track record speaks for itself, with at least 1,000 receiving yards in seven of the past eight seasons – with a torn ACL suffered in the only year he didn’t reach that mark. Dan Quinn knew he was getting a talented player capable of producing even in his early 30s. Washington’s head coach has learned even more about Diggs, since he reported to camp, and his impact on the team. Dan Quinn has been impressed with the fire Stefon Diggs has brought to the team, and said, "the tape is the tape" when it comes to the on-field work. "I knew he was good zones. He's probably better at beating man-to-man than I thought just from the good route running" pic.twitter.com/ZBZZqBfRgm — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) September 2, 2026 “I knew he was a good competitor,” Quinn told reporters after Wednesday’s practice . “I didn’t know how (big) the fire was around others, the skill work in the huddle. He’s the one saying, ‘Let’s go, we’re gonna bah, bah, bah,’ – you can fill in the letters and the words. The fire he has in him – the tape is the tape. The skills as a competitor (are there). I knew he was good in zones. He’s probably better beating man-to-man than I thought, with good route running. I do like the competitor a lot. I really do.” Diggs has made a positive impact on his position group and the Commanders offense overall, well beyond what will eventually show up in the box score. That impact is a bonus, providing more than maybe what Washington hoped for upon signing. It was clear in Diggs’ introductory press conference that the receiver was excited to represent his home region at this stage of his career. He was also pumped to work with Terry McLaurin and a quarterback in Jayden Daniels with star power. That off-the-field presence has been felt by younger players, which should only serve to improve the entire group. “I’ve got great examples in front of me,” second-year receiver Jaylin Lane said, via video from the Commanders . “Adding Diggs is great and added even more veteran experience. I’m just trying to be a sponge and soak up everything and continue to get better.”

(Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 2 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Official gear from The Original Hogs is live. Hats, merch, from the line that set the standard for the offensive line and brought home three Super Bowls. https://t.co/3HZHO7HM22 — Joe Jacoby (@JoeJacoby66HOG) September 1, 2026 Articles Too Deep Zone Aaron Donald: Good. Commanders: Bad. Ravens … Confusing. (Mailbag Pt. 1) Commanders Questions It feels like Washington may be a sneaky contender for “worst team in the league” this year. We all know the Browns and Dolphins stink; why will Washington be worse? – Kevin Langstaff Reader Brutus Rugburn chimed in: Kevin, I agree completely. Looking at their schedule, 3 wins should be the over/under mark. The miracle of 2024 completely screwed up any reasonable, orderly rebuild. Mike, to add to Kevin’s query, how, if at all, could Washington have responded differently to their winning 2024 season with the clearly deficient roster they had? The Commanders are projected to win 7.7 games by DVOA. I think they have had a miserable offseason, despite adding Stefon Diggs. The cavalcade of 32-year old acquisitions I have been dunking on all summer leaves me with little faith about the quality of the front office and the lower tiers of the roster. Dire tales from joint practices make me wonder about the reconfigured coaching staff. So I think the Commanders could be the worst team in the NFL. It’s hard to project them with the worst record, because the Browns quarterback situation is so dire that the team could surrender at the trade deadline, while the Cardinals schedule is so brutal. Relitigating what the Commanders did after reaching the NFC Championship Game in 2024 is tricky. It’s easy to condemn the Laremy Tunsil and Deebo Samuel trades, but those moves made sense at the time. The Commanders got so little besides Jayden Daniels from the 2024 draft that the seeds of decline may have already been sewn. The Commanders needed to do a better job self-scouting the bottom half of their roster and creating competition among younger players in 2025 and this offseason. They should have stockpiled late-round picks and UDFAs and given the ones they did have better opportunities to win roster spots and roles. One or two come-from-nowhere contributors would make their roster look a lot less like the result of an end-of-free-agency shopping spree. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN 2026 NFL bold predictions: Potential surprises for 32 teams Washington Commanders Don’t be surprised if … quarterback Jayden Daniels struggles to regain his brilliant rookie-year form. What I’m hearing: This isn’t about Daniels himself. He’s an absolutely awesome player, and assuming he can get through the season healthy, I expect him to perform at a high level. It’s what’s around him that has me concerned. He has a thin and aging group of wide receivers. He has question marks at running back. And the offensive line issues, especially with left tackle Laremy Tunsil going down with a training camp injury , are too significant to overlook. Earlier in the offseason, I was high on the Commanders’ chances to rebound and contend in the NFC East. But the concerns that arose during camp are giving me pause. The fact that they have a young, first-time offensive coordinator in David Blough adds to the mystery (as, to be fair, it does with the first-time OC in Philadelphia and the first-time defensive coordinator in Dallas). There could be significant growing pains early in the season, if not longer. And even if things work out better than they look right now, Daniels’ 2024 rookie season was one of the best we’ve ever seen. Washington could be pretty good and still not bounce back to that level. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) NFL execs rank NFC teams: Rams, Seahawks clear favorites 13. Washington Commanders Votes: 13-12-13-14-9-13 | Avg: 12.3 | Median: 13 | Vegas wins: 7.5 (T-11th-NFC) Tier votes: Division contender: 1 | Sub-.500: 4 | Top-10 pick: 1 The voter highest on Washington thought Jayden Daniels’ return to health was enough to lift a Commanders team that has question marks entering coach Dan Quinn’s third season, including first-time coordinators on offense (David Blough) and defense (Daronte Jones). “They get Jayden back, and Terry McLaurin will be healthy,” this exec said. “They’ve added some really good parts defensively in free agency. They have to get the offensive line solidified.” Left tackle Laremy Tunsil’s season-ending injury will not help. “I think they are going to be bad,” another exec said. “The quarterback is talented, but his style of play, unless he changes it, is a concern. The weapons around him are OK, but I don’t think it’s a dynamic team offensively. Defensively, they plateaued.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) Jayden Daniels is ready for a new offense. His first task: Learn how to huddle Last season the median NFL offense huddled about 82 percent of the time. When Daniels was on the field, the Commanders huddled about 32 percent of the time. If you remove the first play of the drive (when almost every team huddles), that number plummets to 20 percent. Taking away huddles after timeouts or penalties would drop it even more. For all intents and purposes, Daniels has never huddled play-to-play in his pro career. Kliff Kingsbury’s offense the last two seasons didn’t require it, but Daniels also didn’t do it in college. Without a huddle, there is less information a quarterback can communicate to the other 10 players. That lends itself to a less complex offense, one that’s easier for defenses to decipher. Tempo typically offsets some of that. Even if you have a simpler offense, going quickly can create an edge. Instead, the Commanders self-neutralized their inherent advantage. Last year, on average, there were 9.6 seconds remaining on the playclock when the Commanders snapped the ball, eighth-highest in the NFL and much closer to the league average (9 seconds) than the Dallas Cowboys’ league-leading 12 seconds. Commanders coaches know Daniels is going to run — they just don’t have to call it. Quinn estimates Daniels will have four or five rushing attempts off scrambles alone each game. Adding designed runs to that “is how you end up with 10,” Quinn says. The league’s average quarterback scramble rate the past two seasons is 5.5 percent. Daniels sits atop the NFL at 13.8 percent, multiple percentage points ahead of runners-up like Justin Fields, Tyler Huntley and Drake Maye. So Washington has to set up some guardrails. And this is the biggest reason why Daniels will be under center more often this year. Getting under center should, in theory, make defenses respect the play-action game more than shotgun, where sometimes defenders can see the entire exchange (or lack thereof). That will help Daniels as a passer, as defenses have to play the run more honestly, and help the run game be more explosive. Just like the huddle, no team the last two seasons has been under center less often than the Commanders. Last year Washington was under center just 13.1 percent of the time, and that dropped to 5.8 percent when Daniels was on the field. The Cincinnati Bengals had the second-lowest percentage of plays under center (18.4). With one training camp and three preseason snaps in the books, Daniels hasn’t decided on whether to stand up, hunch over or take a knee [in the huddle]. “It might depend,” Daniels tells…

title: NFL players, coaches, GMs under the most pressure in 2026
summary: Can Baker Mayfield and C.J. Stroud play their way to big contracts? Is Aaron Glenn on thin ice with the Jets? Which 2024 first-rounders have fifth-year options at stake?
full_text:
Some people around the NFL have more riding on the 2026 season than others. The vast majority of players are on one-year deals or have limited or no guaranteed money waiting for them in 2027. Every coordinator and assistant coach is one bad year away from potentially looking for work. And although a fair number of head coaches and general managers have real job security, others might have a storied career with one team come down to a missed field goal or a contested catch at the wrong time -- to which John Harbaugh and Sean McDermott can attest.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Today, I'm looking at the players, coaches and executives who might be most impacted by what they do -- or don't do -- during the 2026 campaign. Perhaps it is a player in position to make life-changing money if he has a good season at the right time. Perhaps it is someone on the verge of losing their path to a starting role. It could also mean coaches and executives looking to lock up another contract with a successful year.

 Even within this group, though, there are a few players who could really see their future diverge into one of two dramatically different paths solely based on what they do over the next 17 games. Let's open things up there. Here are 23 people around the NFL with the most to gain or lose in 2026.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Stroud | Pickens | Mayfield | Murray 
 Three coordinators | Porter | Jones 
 Colts brass | Hunter | Wilson | Glenn 
 Fifth-year options | Hall of Fame candidates 

 
 

 

 C.J. Stroud , QB, Houston Texans 
 I'll start with the player who might have a wider range of outcomes heading into the season than anyone. There aren't many candidates in any given year who have a shot at coming out of the campaign as the highest-paid player in NFL history. But Stroud has the potential to be that player if things go right. There's also a world where things go south and he's competing for his job -- or on another roster altogether -- in 2027.

 In a what-have-you-done-for-me-lately sports universe, Stroud's disastrous postseason has dominated offseason discussion around the fourth-year pro. Turning the ball over seven times (and being lucky to avoid more) in two games will do that. Texans fans will look at what the Seahawks did on the other side of the bracket, with a dominant defense and a quarterback who avoided turning the ball over at all in three games, and rue what happened in January. Between teams such as the Chiefs and Ravens missing the playoffs altogether, and the Broncos showing up in the AFC Championship Game without their starting quarterback, the 2025 season might go down as a missed opportunity for the Texans.

 

 The Texans should feel like Super Bowl contenders again in 2026, given that they return virtually everyone of note on an elite defense, but there's unquestionable anxiety about Stroud. Perhaps that's unwarranted. Stroud posted a 61.7 QBR during the 2025 regular season, which was good for 11th in the league, ahead of quarterbacks such as  Trevor Lawrence and Bo Nix . He did that with inconsistent offensive line play and a moribund run game, issues that have plagued Houston throughout Stroud's first three seasons in the NFL.

 My concern is that those issues haven't really been resolved. General manager Nick Caserio has churned through running back and offensive line changes yet again this offseason, but there are still legitimate questions about the sort of help Stroud will receive. Veterans Braden Smith and Wyatt Teller haven't been able to carve out starting roles, and Smith could miss a few weeks with a plantar fascia injury . New lead back David Montgomery  is moving from one of the most run-friendly offenses in the league to one of its least in terms of expected yards per carry. And wideout Jayden Higgins is already out for the year after tearing an ACL , leading the Texans to trade for Kayshon Boutte , who will have to learn the offense on the fly.

 That might be the most realistic shift between the Stroud some saw as a rookie and the one who hasn't significantly built on that impressive debut campaign. He needs help. Stroud might not be able to single-handedly propel the offense forward in the way that the league's true high-end quarterbacks can. That rookie year was built on an unsustainable interception rate (1.0%) and an impressive penchant for picking up chunks of yardage (8.2 yards per attempt). Stroud hasn't been close to either number since then.

 The 2024-25 version of Stroud is still a very solid starter, and I'd argue he hasn't gotten much support, but that's a different player with a different ceiling from the one who immediately propelled the Texans into contention in 2023. There's nothing wrong with this version of Stroud, and if the Texans haven't resolved the infrastructure issues surrounding him this offseason, it's where Stroud is likely to settle by the end of the 2026 season. But if the run game finally gets going, I still believe Stroud has another level, and a season like his 2023 campaign might be enough to earn the young QB the biggest contract in NFL history.

 If the postseason issues linger into the 2027 season and the Texans disappoint, would the Texans be willing to consider what life looks like without Stroud on what could be a franchise-limiting second contract? The difference between those two scenarios might be $100 million or more in guaranteed money.

 

 
 

 George Pickens , WR, Dallas Cowboys 
 Prove it. That was the mantra for Pickens heading into the 2025 season, after the Steelers clearly decided that they didn't want to move forward with their mercurial wideout on a significant contract extension. Pittsburgh dealt Pickens to the Cowboys for a Day 2 pick, and with a major upgrade at quarterback, he produced a career season. Pickens set career highs in receptions (93), receiving yards (1,429) and touchdowns (nine), earning his first trip to the Pro Bowl.

 Prove it again. The Cowboys also weren't willing to sign Pickens to a long-term contract after the season, instead using the franchise tag to retain his services on a one-year, $27.3 million pact. Were the Cowboys concerned about their ability to keep Pickens motivated? Were they unwilling to commit significant money to a second receiver given what they're already paying Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb ? Or did they just not believe that Pickens' 2025 season represented what he'll do moving forward?

 

 Some combination of the three might be true, but if Pickens can produce a repeat season, it won't matter. The Cowboys spent heavily to fix their defense this offseason, and they might not be interested in a second franchise tag for Pickens in 2027, which would cost more than $32 million. Hitting unrestricted free agency as a 26-year-old wide receiver could be a massive opportunity for Pickens, who would potentially be the best player available.

 

 
 

 Baker Mayfield , QB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 The " Baker Mayfield Rule " holds that the veteran quarterback's performance is inversely correlated with how much confidence the public has in his ability. More doubt, more success. As soon as Mayfield started earning consideration as an MVP candidate around the midway point of the 2025 season, his performance cratered, taking Tampa Bay's season along for the ride.

 Are the Bucs testing this corollary by refusing to come to terms with the pending 2027 unrestricted free agent on a contract extension? He unquestionably exceeded the initial expectations on him when he joined Tampa Bay to compete with Kyle Trask for the starting job. Mayfield hasn't missed a start in three years, he won a playoff game over the Eagles in 2023, and he ranks 14th in QBR over his run with the Bucs, between quarterbacks such as  Jared Goff (12th) and Trevor Lawrence (16th). Goff makes $53 million per year, while Lawrence is at $55 million. You can understand why Mayfield wants to be in a ballpark with his fellow former first overall picks, and given cap…

title: Who calls plays for every NFL team in 2026? What to know
summary: From veterans to newbies, here's everything you need to know about the NFL's playcallers in 2026.
full_text:
The 2026 season kicks off in six days with a rematch of Super Bowl LX, as the reigning champion Seattle Seahawks host the New England Patriots on Wednesday ( 8:20 p.m. ET, NBC ).

 Josh McDaniels returns as the Patriots' playcaller. On the other side of the field, Brian Fleury replaces Seattle's 2025 offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak, who became the Las Vegas Raiders ' head coach this offseason, making him one of 18 new offensive playcallers this season.

 Veteran head coaches Andy Reid ( Kansas City Chiefs ), Kyle Shanahan ( San Francisco 49ers ) and Sean McVay ( Los Angeles Rams ) continue to make the calls in their creative offensive systems, but Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton surprisingly handed over playcalling duties to offensive coordinator Davis Webb.

 Meanwhile, some old faces have resurfaced in new places, including Mike McCarthy as Pittsburgh Steelers head coach, Frank Reich calling plays for the New York Jets , Brian Daboll as OC with the Tennessee Titans and Mike McDaniel as the Los Angeles Chargers ' OC.

 That doesn't even account for first-time playcallers, such as Baltimore Ravens OC Declan Doyle, Philadelphia Eagles OC Sean Mannion and Washington Commanders OC David Blough.

 With so many changes heading into 2026, here is a look at who is calling plays for all 32 teams, plus a key stat provided by ESPN Research.

 Jump to: 
 ARI  | ATL  | BAL  | BUF  | CAR  | CHI  |  CIN 
 CLE  | DAL  | DEN  | DET  | GB  | HOU  | IND 
 JAX  | KC  | LAC  | LAR | LV | MIA  | MIN 
 NE  | NO  | NYG  | NYJ  | PHI  | PIT  | SF 
 SEA  | TB  | TEN  | WSH 

 

 AFC EAST 
 

 

 Buffalo Bills 
 Playcaller:  Joe Brady, head coach

 Experience:  Brady has called plays for quarterback Josh Allen since mid-November 2023, going from interim offensive coordinator to offensive coordinator and now calling plays while taking over as head coach. He also called plays on the NFL level in his nearly two seasons with the Carolina Panthers .

 What to know:  While Brady has significant experience calling plays, he's a first-time head coach. He'll have the challenge of managing both jobs at once, while leading a team with high expectations. Success has been consistent with Brady calling plays for the Allen-led offense in Buffalo, as the Bills are second in points per game (29.6) and first in offensive EPA since 2024. A change, however, for the offense under Brady this season is that former tight ends coach Rob Boras is run game coordinator. -- Alaina Getzenberg 

 Key stat:  The Bills designed runs on 59% of their first-down plays since Brady took over offensive playcalling duties in November 2023 (highest percentage in NFL) after designing rushes on 42% of first downs in Allen's career before Brady took over (lowest percentage in NFL).  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 Miami Dolphins 
 Playcaller:  Bobby Slowik, offensive coordinator

 Experience: This is Slowik's second season with the Dolphins after spending 2025 as the team's passing game coordinator. He previously spent two seasons as the Houston Texans ' offensive coordinator.

 What to know:  The Dolphins' poor passing game in 2025 could be attributed to a decline in quarterback play, an injury to WR  Tyreek Hill and lack of legitimate options once Hill went down. Slowik's first season in Houston coincided with QB  C.J. Stroud 's rookie season, when Stroud was named AP Rookie of the Year and the Texans finished seventh in passing yards. The production tapered off the following season and the Texans finished 22nd in total yards. Slowik will tailor this Dolphins offense around running back De'Von Achane and quarterback Malik Willis -- who offers a more dynamic skill set than any quarterback he has ever worked with. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques 

 Key stat:  The Dolphins recorded the NFL's second-highest screen attempt percentage (14%) last season with Slowik as senior passing game coordinator.  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 New England Patriots 
 Playcaller: Josh McDaniels, offensive coordinator

 Experience: In his 25th NFL season and 20th with the Patriots, McDaniels enters his 15th year as the team's offensive coordinator (three different stints). McDaniels turned 50 on April 22.

 What to know:  One of the themes of training camp has been QB Drake Maye taking more ownership of the offense because it's his second year in McDaniels' system. McDaniels leads an experienced offensive staff that includes former NFL head coaches and/or coordinators in Doug Marrone (offensive line), Thomas Brown (tight ends/passing game coordinator) and Todd Downing (wide receivers). -- Mike Reiss 

 Key stat:  The Patriots had the second-highest average pass distance in the NFL last season (8.7), the highest rate for a McDaniels-led offense since 2017 (8.8 with Patriots).  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 New York Jets 
 Playcaller:  Frank Reich, offensive coordinator

 Experience:  It's his first season with the Jets, but Reich is a seasoned playcaller -- having handled the responsibility for the Chargers, Colts and Panthers.

 What to know:  It'll be interesting to see if Reich, 64, back in the league after a two-year hiatus, has added any wrinkles to his system. His last two seasons (2023-24 in Carolina) weren't good. His biggest challenge is helping quarterback Geno Smith reduce his interceptions. He will lean into the running game and will use more 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 WR, 2 TE) than usual. The Jets finished 29th in scoring, their 10th straight season in the bottom third. Things can only go up, right? -- Rich Cimini 

 Key stat:  The Colts had five receivers in pass routes on 75% of their plays in Reich's tenure as head coach (2018-22), the second-highest percentage in the NFL in that span behind only the Chiefs (77%), per NFL Next Gen Stats.  -- ESPN Research 

 

 AFC NORTH 

 

 

 Baltimore Ravens 
 Playcaller:  Declan Doyle, offensive coordinator

 Experience:  Doyle is calling plays for the first time of his eight-year NFL career. He was the offensive coordinator last season for the Chicago Bears , but head coach Ben Johnson called the plays. Doyle was previously the tight ends coach with the Denver Broncos (2023-24) and an offensive assistant with the New Orleans Saints (2019-22).

 

 What to know:  Doyle, who turned 30 in March, is the youngest playcaller in the league. The players have praised Doyle's system for its details. Quarterback Lamar Jackson said Doyle has been "like a wizard." Wide receiver Zay Flowers has called him "a genius." One of the biggest changes has been putting Jackson under center after he lined up in the pistol for 95% of his NFL career. Doyle has been tough on the two-time NFL Most Valuable Player, from his footwork to his reads. "He's grading me like I'm a rookie or something," Jackson said. "He's always on me. But I appreciate it." -- Jamison Hensley 

 Key stat:  With Doyle as offensive coordinator, Bears QB Caleb Williams had the second-most pass attempts outside the pocket last season (128), trailing Bo Nix (133).  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 Cincinnati Bengals 
 Playcaller:  Zac Taylor, head coach

 Experience: Taylor is entering his eighth year as the Bengals' head coach. He has been the playcaller for all eight seasons.

 What to know:  Taylor's playcalling has come under fire over the years. But whether it was Brian Callahan or Dan Pitcher serving as offensive coordinator, Taylor has held onto the reins. This season, Taylor is looking for new ways to create a more explosive offense, especially with Joe Burrow back under center. Even with Burrow out for nine games last season, Cincinnati finished 13th in points per drive. But the big plays have been lacking, which is a focal point for a unit that features Burrow, wide receivers Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins and running back Chase Brown . -- Ben Baby 

 Key stat:  Over the past four seasons, the Bengals have the highest designed pass percentage in the NFL (67%).  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 Cleveland Browns

title: 2026 NFL bold predictions: Potential surprises for 32 teams
summary: Jameson Williams leading the Lions' receivers? Xavier Worthy breaking out? Travis Hunter almost entirely at CB? We have 32 outside-the-box things to watch.
full_text:
I love surprises. They're my favorite part of sports. People sometimes ask if I'm upset that I got a prediction wrong, and I tend to answer no. If I knew what was going to happen ahead of time, I don't think I'd enjoy watching the games. I watch them because I know they can surprise me. I strongly believe that surprises are the main reason watching sports is fun.

 However, I recognize that not everyone feels this way. Many of you like to have some ability to predict what's going to happen for, let's say, profit-related reasons? Hey, I get it. I play a ton of fantasy football, and surprises can mess with that. I understand the appeal of any information that can help put me in the best possible position to at least anticipate what's likely to happen, if not get all the way to certainty.

 So every year, right before the start of the NFL season, we do this all-32 list in which I go through every team and pick out one potential surprise. This is based on the reporting I've done throughout training camp, talking to people with and around these teams and trying to figure out what the plan is for each franchise. They aren't predictions in the strictest sense. They're more tidbits that I think could signal things you might not be expecting. (They're also generally more informative for people who aren't fans of the specific team to whom they apply. I get that some people follow these teams far more closely than others, and that what might be a surprise to someone on the outside might not be to those who've been gobbling up every training camp play-by-play and news conference sound bite.)

 Anyway, that's enough with the disclaimers. Enjoy these. Come back in a few months and tell me where I was right and where I was wrong. I promise I won't mind even if it's the latter. That's the fun part of the NFL season , after all.

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 NFC EAST 
 

 Dallas Cowboys 
 Don't be surprised if ... rookie safety Caleb Downs never leaves the field. 

 What I'm hearing:  OK, maybe that's a slight exaggeration, but the Cowboys believe they can use Downs in a ton of different ways. In their ideal world, he and veteran safety Jalen Thompson are interchangeable in the safety and nickel roles. Downs got a lot of work at nickel during camp, and Dallas has faith in his ability to play deep safety. The Cowboys believe in his ability to cover top receivers if that's what they need from him, and they think he will be instantly capable of communicating at a high level and helping keep things organized on the defense.

 The Cowboys drafted Downs hoping they could plug and play him on defense in Year 1, and to their absolute delight, he has shown himself to be just that in every situation they've thrown at him so far. They're counting on him to handle a key role in the revitalization of their defense under new coordinator Christian Parker, and I expect him to play a ton.

 

 
 

 

 New York Giants 
 Don't be surprised if ... tight end Isaiah Likely is a breakout star in New York. 

 What I'm hearing:  Giants coaches light up when talking about Likely, the free agent signee who came over from Baltimore with coach John Harbaugh. They believe he'll be a real asset for Jaxson Dart as a receiver and think he can win in both man and zone coverage. And they love the way he has embraced and evolved his relationship with Dart since he has been in New York. Likely is a regular visitor to the quarterbacks room, and the connection he has formed with Dart on and off the field could pay major dividends. Likely is a strong candidate to be the team's second-leading receiver this season and could be even more than that if top wideout Malik Nabers needs time to get up to speed coming off his injury .

 

 
 

 Philadelphia Eagles 
 Don't be surprised if ... they have the best defense in the NFL this season. 

 What I'm hearing:  The questions on offense in Philadelphia are myriad and totally legitimate. The new coordinator, Sean Mannion, is a first-time playcaller and in just his third year as a coach at any level. Longtime offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland's departure leaves a void, too. The Eagles also traded their best receiver to the Patriots in  A.J. Brown . And on and on. Regardless, the Vic Fangio defense should be an absolute monster.

 Sure, the Jonathan Greenard   pec strain  is a blow to the pass rush, but he shouldn't be out too long, and the Eagles expect guys such as  Moro Ojomo to contribute there in the meantime.  Jihaad Campbell should make an impact in his second season at linebacker, too. The secondary, fortified by the free agent addition of Riq Woolen , is ascending and already Super Bowl-tested. The interior defensive line duo of Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis is a strength. And the continuity under Fangio is a big reason to believe this unit will only be better. The Eagles look like the kind of defense that can carry a transitioning offense through early-season growing pains.

 

 
 

 Washington Commanders 
 Don't be surprised if ... quarterback Jayden Daniels struggles to regain his brilliant rookie-year form. 

 What I'm hearing: This isn't about Daniels himself. He's an absolutely awesome player, and assuming he can get through the season healthy, I expect him to perform at a high level. It's what's around him that has me concerned. He has a thin and aging group of wide receivers. He has question marks at running back. And the offensive line issues, especially with left tackle  Laremy Tunsil  going down with a training camp injury , are too significant to overlook.

 Earlier in the offseason, I was high on the Commanders' chances to rebound and contend in the NFC East. But the concerns that arose during camp are giving me pause. The fact that they have a young, first-time offensive coordinator in David Blough adds to the mystery (as, to be fair, it does with the first-time OC in Philadelphia and the first-time defensive coordinator in Dallas). There could be significant growing pains early in the season, if not longer. And even if things work out better than they look right now, Daniels' 2024 rookie season was one of the best we've ever seen. Washington could be pretty good and still not bounce back to that level.

 

 

 NFC NORTH 
 

 Chicago Bears 
 Don't be surprised if ... the Bears still trade for an edge rusher. 

 What I'm hearing:  Chicago is thin on defense, especially on the back end. But it's up front where the team is still looking for a strong edge presence opposite Montez Sweat . The Bears added veteran Marcus Davenport a couple of weeks ago, but that move doesn't appear to be working out; they let Davenport go in their initial cut down to 53 players over the weekend before bringing him back on the practice squad. Bears GM Ryan Poles has been an active and aggressive trader in his time with the team, and he'll turn over every rock he can looking for an impact player up front. The Bears' health issues on defense might be more concentrated on the back end, but improving the pass rush would help the secondary, too.

 

 
 

 Detroit Lions 
 Don't be surprised if ...  Jameson Williams is the team's leading receiver. 

 What I'm hearing:  No disrespect to Amon-Ra St. Brown , one of the most consistent pass catchers in the entire league. But I think this Lions offense is going to hum this season, and Williams is the player poised to take the biggest leap. For a few years now, the coaching staff has been pushing Williams to expand his route repertoire and contribute as more than just a deep threat. And in Drew Petzing's offense, Williams could be poised to do just that. The Lions' schedule of opposing defenses sets up well for Williams, and if he proves himself to be a trustworthy target for Jared Goff , he could be in for a career year.

title: 11 NFL players to watch next offseason -- if they don't sign extensions
summary: From C.J. Stroud to top cornerbacks, we go through players up for extensions who could also be on the move in 2027.
full_text:
Player contracts are accelerating at an Xavier Worthy -esque pace this offseason. The past six months have triggered an avalanche of market-topping deals, from a quarterback making $64 million per year ( Patrick Mahomes ) to an edge rusher earning an annual average of $50 million ( Will Anderson Jr. ).

 Five players have become positional cash kings this summer alone, with several more setting high marks back in the spring. Since June, five defensive tackles have earned deals worth at least $30 million per year.

 Some teams privately grumble over ballooning salaries and the inherent challenges of building a competitive team around star players who eat up much of their salary cap. But the soaring costs simply parallel a 44.7% increase in the NFL's cap over the past four years, from $208.2 million in 2022 to $301.2 million now.

 The previous four-year spike was 17.4%, from $177.2 million in 2018 to the 2022 number, and while the pandemic stalled progress, nothing is slowing down what's happening now. But many elite players still need new deals with Week 1 just days away. Some will get to the finish line before kickoff; some won't.

 ESPN made calls around the league to provide the latest information on many of the key contract extension candidates: Who gets paid and who will strategically wait things out until the offseason?

 
 Jump to a topic: 
 Lamar Jackson  | C.J. Stroud 
 Christian Gonzalez  | Joey Porter Jr. 
 DJ Turner  | Quenton Nelson 
 Tucker Kraft  | Detroit duo 

 
 

 

 

 Lamar Jackson , QB, Baltimore Ravens 
 Jackson, to his credit, is fiercely private about his negotiations. And as his own agent, he has proved to be a shrewd negotiator. Just look back at 2023, when Jackson remained patient, requested a trade after being franchise-tagged and finally landed a five-year, $260 million deal.

 It's no surprise this negotiation is void of many details. But the league sentiment is this: Jackson has massive leverage and appears ready to use it, which means the chances of him playing out 2026 without an extension could grow by the day.

 

 He is owed $52 million in cash in each of the next two seasons with an $84.3 million cap hit in 2027, which might as well be a poison pill. He has a no-franchise-tag provision and a no-trade clause. If he wants to entertain a new home outside of Baltimore in future years, he has full control of where it is -- especially if he has another banner season.

 Perhaps Baltimore gives Jackson an offer he can't refuse soon. But he can sit tight and let the market do the work for him next offseason, when several star quarterbacks from the 2024 draft class will be eligible for extensions.

 Perhaps then Jackson will become the NFL's first player to earn $70 million per year.

 

 

 

 C.J. Stroud , QB, Houston Texans 
 Several people with knowledge of the situation believe Stroud is prepared to play out this season without a new deal, despite Houston making what it considered a competitive offer.

 There's still time before kickoff to reach a deal -- and the Texans' front office is aggressive in re-signing core players -- but the current sentiment is Stroud will most likely not end up with a new deal.

 My understanding is Houston is prepared to put Stroud in what it feels is a strong place among the 12 quarterbacks in the $50 million club.

 But like Jackson, Stroud can let an exploding quarterback market do the work for him if he waits an additional six to eight months. By all accounts, Stroud had a strong training camp and believes he can rebound from last season's struggles. Houston is squarely in the Super Bowl discussion based on its talent level and elite defense. There's a lot for Stroud to gain -- and potentially lose -- by delaying a deal. He has had moments of brilliance since entering the league in 2023. Channeling that brilliance while properly managing the game will go a long way.

 On Tuesday, Texans general manager Nick Caserio set a Week 1 deadline for a deal with Stroud .

 

 "If we don't get it figured out before the season starts, then it'll be something we address in the offseason," Caserio said.

 

 

 Christian Gonzalez , CB, New England Patriots 
 On the surface, this deal feels like a no-brainer. Gonzalez was the No. 3 cornerback as ranked by executives, coaches and scouts , a true press-man coverage player who dominated late last season. He has an All-Pro and a Pro Bowl nod.  Seattle Seahawks corner Devon Witherspoon 's four-year, $132 million deal set the table.

 But this one is taking a while to reach a conclusion. Gonzalez did not appear thrilled when addressing local media members this summer. Perhaps that had something to do with team owner Robert Kraft floating publicly at the start of camp that New England offered to make Gonzalez the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history.

 My understanding of this situation is that if Gonzalez were to sign a market-setting deal -- and it will need to be just that -- then it has to be buttoned up. And the sides are not close on several elements of the deal.

 

 It's worth noting New England hasn't executed many recent top-line extensions from which to draw. Rob Gronkowski's six-year, $54 million extension in 2012 was the highest for a tight end at the time but was considered team friendly due to the number of years. Tom Brady was famously underpaid. New England has spent big on free agents but not necessarily on many market-resetting extensions. Gonzalez, who as of now does not plan to negotiate during the season, is testing that in a big way.

 

 

 Joey Porter Jr. , CB, Pittsburgh Steelers 
 This is probably the most complicated of them all. Momentum for a deal just hasn't been there. My sense is the player has been frustrated that, despite his status as a high-level man corner, he hasn't been made a priority. The 2023 draft picks getting paid by Pittsburgh -- linebacker  Nick Herbig and defensive tackle  Keeanu Benton , who received four-year extensions this summer -- play smaller roles.

 

 Sources say the Steelers' lack of a formal offer for weeks sent the clear message to Porter that they would like him to play out the final year of his rookie contract, which prompted him to consider the possibility of a trade or sitting out for an extended period. The 26-year-old stayed away from the practice field for weeks but returned Tuesday. Perhaps his participation ignites talks, but he's leaving that up to his agents .

 The semantics are this: The Steelers most likely would do a deal with Porter. But the mechanics of the cornerback market (as outlined above with Gonzalez) are hard to ignore. Five cornerbacks make $30 million or more per year. After that, there's a drop to $25 million (the  Carolina Panthers '  Jaycee Horn ). Porter essentially has to pick which group he thinks he belongs in, and all indications are it's not the latter. And the Steelers might not want him in the former on their dime.

 

 The Steelers don't negotiate during the season, which fuels the urgency over the coming week.

 I'm told the new coaching staff is not a deterrent here. They are all-in on his ability as a high-level cover man.

 Another hurdle: The 2027 franchise tag at cornerback is a below-market $23 million.

 

 

 DJ Turner , CB, Cincinnati Bengals 
 Like Porter, Turner is an underrated cover man out of the AFC North. But this deal has virtually no chance to get done before Week 1, barring a massive and unexpected uptick. It isn't close, and Turner is poised to play out his rookie deal.

 If Cincinnati follows its own blueprint, it will franchise-tag Turner as it did with another star defensive back, Jessie Bates III , in 2022. Bates had to play on the tag, before reaching a four-year deal with the  Atlanta Falcons  in free agency.

 

 Turner will be in line for a large payday in free agency, if he reaches it. But the franchise tag is a real possibility here.

title: As opener nears, Falcons still have not announced a QB1
summary: GM Ian Cunningham spoke Wednesday, and the only update he gave is that selecting the starting QB will be a group effort.
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- The Atlanta Falcons still don't know who their starting quarterback will be for their Week 1 opener at the  Pittsburgh Steelers  on Sept. 13, or least they're not yet saying.

 One thing they do know, though, is the decision will not be made by one individual.

 Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham said Wednesday it will be a group effort that includes himself, head coach Kevin Stefanski, president of football Matt Ryan and owner Arthur Blank.

 "We all talk about it," Cunningham said. "We all have been talking about it forever. So, at the end of the day, we'll make the decision, and when it's time to make the decision, we'll let you know."

 

 Michael Penix Jr . was the team's starting quarterback for Week 1 last season. But he tore his left ACL last November and did not get cleared to practice fully until last week. Penix did not play in any preseason games and only started work in 11-on-11 periods on Aug. 24.

 The Falcons signed Tua Tagovailoa to a one-year, $1.3 million contract in the offseason following his release from the Miami Dolphins  in early March. Tagovailoa came into training camp in late July with a tight back and missed about a week. So he, like Penix, also faced a setback.

 With Tagovailoa and Penix out, all the early reps in practice went to veteran Cooper Rush (whom the Falcons signed just a day before camp began) and undrafted rookie Jack Strand . Rush and Strand both performed well in the preseason and the Falcons decided to keep all four quarterbacks on the 53-man roster earlier this week.

 "So, it just so happens that we had four guys who went out and earned it at that position and it's a good position to have depth," assistant general manager Jeff Scott said. "So, as far as I'm concerned, it's about whoever goes out there works and earns it."

 

 The Falcons are keeping their decision-making process relatively close to the vest. While most figure that either Penix or Tagovailoa will be the starter, Cunningham would not say Wednesday that Rush and Strand were out of contention.

 "I can't answer that," Cunningham said.

 One thing Cunningham was able to answer was that the Falcons brain trust wants to see more of Penix. He had just three practices doing 11-on-11s last week and the team wants as much data as it can get before making a decision.

 "The more reps, the more evaluations we can get, the better," Cunningham said. "Just like we discussed, that's the hand that we were dealt. So, the more opportunities that we can to evaluate, the better it is. "

title: How Ravens' Henry is driven to rank among NFL's best backs
summary: Henry has made it clear this summer that this season will not be his last. But this season will likely be a momentous one nonetheless.
full_text:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- In a sideline interview during the Baltimore Ravens ' preseason game at the  Minnesota Vikings , running back  Derrick Henry  was asked how his body feels going into his 11th NFL season. 
 
 "Let's do 11 more," Henry said with a chuckle. 
 
 Henry has made it clear this summer that this season will not be his last. But this season will likely be a momentous one nonetheless. 
 
 Henry, who ranks 10th on the NFL's all-time rushing list, is 994 yards away from leapfrogging his way to No. 6. He could surpass four Hall of Fame running backs -- Eric Dickerson, Jerome Bettis, LaDainian Tomlinson and Curtis Martin -- who combined for 11 first-team All-Pro selections and seven single-season rushing titles. 
 
 
 
 If Henry can rush for 1,811 yards this season, which he has surpassed twice in his career (most recently in his debut season with the Ravens in 2024), he would move past Adrian Peterson for No. 5 on the list. 
 
 Running back Justice Hill , who is Henry's primary backup, smiled when asked whether Henry knows how many yards he needs to climb the league's career rushing ranks. 
 
 "He's well aware of where he stands right now," Hill said. "And he's well aware of what he needs to get to get in the top five because we talk about it." 
 
 Hill added, "When you go into a season, you always talk about your goals and things you're trying to achieve. And even though he's not going to talk about it out here, it's definitely a striving factor for him." 
 
 Henry made a big jump last season, going from No. 19 on the all-time rushing list to No. 10. When Henry eclipsed Tony Dorsett to move into the top 10 in December, he said, "It's a surreal moment for me and something that I always cherish." 
 
 
 
 In Henry's two seasons in Baltimore, he has led the NFL in rushing yards (3,516) and carries (632). This season, Henry will be playing in a new offensive system, but that is nothing new for him. 
 
 Declan Doyle, who replaced Todd Monken as the playcaller in Baltimore, is Henry's eighth offensive coordinator of his 11-year career. Doyle wouldn't commit to Henry getting over 300 carries for a third straight year but indicated Henry will have "an immense role." 
 
 "He's going to have a pretty large workload," Doyle said. "I was telling the offensive staff how cool it is when you call a run play [as a] first-time playcaller and Derrick Henry is the running back, and you're like, 'The odds of this working are a lot higher.'" 
 
 Other attainable milestones for Henry include: 
 
 He needs two rushing touchdowns to surpass Marcus Allen (123) for third on the NFL's all-time list. 
 He can tie Tomlinson for the most consecutive seasons and most total seasons with at least 10 rushing touchdowns in NFL history (10). 
 He can surpass Barry Sanders (five) for the most seasons with at least 1,500 rushing yards in league history. 
 
 
 
 
 Henry's teammates believe his work ethic is even more impressive than his numbers. 
 
 "What this guy has been able to do, we all know -- first-ballot [Hall of Famer]. Who he is as a person -- I've never seen the guy complain," linebacker Roquan Smith said. "[He] comes in day in, day out, grinds, never takes the easy route. I am just truly happy to have him on my team now and not have to worry about going against him." 
 
 When Smith previously had to go head-to-head with Henry, Smith acknowledged that all you think about all week is going against "The King." 
 
 "Like, he's -- 6-foot-3, 6-4, 260 [pounds], whatever he weighs -- [and he looks like] a Greek god," Smith said. "So, you were definitely going down there making sure you had your chin strap maybe a little tight, a little extra air in your helmet and everything like that." 
 
 In addition to ascending the NFL's career rushing yards, Henry has become the benchmark for durability among running backs. He's the active leader with 2,662 career carries, which are 822 more than any other current running back. 
 
 Henry scoffed this summer when asked about whether he has contemplated retirement. When he recently told a podcast that he would like to finish his career with the Ravens, he felt it got misconstrued that he was soon calling it quits. 
 
 Henry wrote on social media: "I never said anything about retiring lol , I'm enjoying being a Raven . I'll worry about that retirement s--- later ." 
 
 Ravens offensive tackle Ronnie Stanley said no one should try to predict when Henry is walking away from the game. 
 
 "As long as he is having fun and he feels good, he could play as long as he wants because they do not build humans like that," Stanley said. 
 
 
 
 So could Henry eventually become the NFL's all-time rushing champion? He's 5,337 yards behind Emmitt Smith, who ran for a league-best 18,355 in his 15-year career. 
 
 If Henry plays five more seasons (including this one) to equal Smith, he would need to average 1,068 yards each year to capture the No. 1 spot. 
 
 Hill thinks Henry can do it. 
 
 "There's no end in sight for him," Hill said. "You talk to some guys, and they're like, 'I get one more good season, maybe two more.' You couldn't tell that with Derrick . He might play another five years."

title: How Panthers QB Bryce Young, playcaller Brad Idzik will mesh in 2026
summary: Carolina believes a more aggressive approach under first-time playcaller Brad Idzik can help franchise QB Bryce Young reach another level.
full_text:
THE CAROLINA PANTHERS ' starting offense slumped to start the 2026 NFL preseason. Fourth-year quarterback Bryce Young and offensive coordinator Brad Idzik hadn't found their footing. The offense managed 26 total yards in its first four drives together.

 But on the fifth drive, against the Jacksonville Jaguars' backup defense in the second week of the preseason at EverBank Stadium, Idzik, Young and the Panthers adjusted for a seven-play, 58-yard touchdown drive. Young moved around the pocket and made quick tosses down the field to tight end Tommy Tremble and wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan , and the offense as a whole functioned with urgency during the series.

 It was a glimmer. It was a glimpse of how this offense can operate with Young and Idzik leading a new, more aggressive charge heading into the 2026 regular season that begins with the Panthers hosting the Chicago Bears on Sept. 13 ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ).

 Idzik is new to playcalling, but he's not new to Young. The coordinator, now in his third year with the title, will take control of those playcalling duties after inheriting the job from coach Dave Canales this offseason. And with a new voice in the quarterback's helmet on game days, the hope is that Young -- with a lucrative contract extension at stake -- will flourish during the biggest season of his NFL career and the Panthers will make another postseason run.

 "He's definitely been aggressive, which is huge for us," Young said about Idzik and his ability to guide the QB and the game. "That's a part of the offense we can build upon and we can expand in. We have the guys -- I have all the faith in the world in our guys out there. So giving them opportunities down the field; try to be more explosive, more dynamic."

 
 THE YOUNG-LED CAROLINA offense failed to get off to fast starts over the past two seasons with Canales calling plays.

 According to TruMedia, the Panthers' offense ranked 21st and 26th in first-quarter scoring average in each of the past two seasons, respectively. While Carolina had the 15th-ranked first-quarter time of possession average in 2024, that status dropped to 29th in 2025.

 

 The team has won five total games in the first eight weeks of the past two seasons during the Canales era, partially because the offense hasn't gotten off to hot starts on Sundays, especially before the calendar flips to November.

 But after finishing 30th in passing yardage and 29th in total yardage in 2024, and 26th and 27th in those respective categories in 2025, Carolina wants to push the tempo with Idzik at the controls.

 In theory, a quick and efficient procedure should allow the Panthers to control the momentum when Young is directing traffic on the field.

 "The biggest thing, and I think this would come in Year 3 -- whether I was calling it or Dave was -- is the aggressive nature of the pre-snap, breaking the huddle, getting to the line, and having confidence in if we're not checking a play, let's get this thing rolling," Idzik said. "Let's roll off the ball and put the defense on their heels."

 Training camp was the time to test the tandem's focus on urgency. And while the summer might have been a fun return to football for Idzik, Young and the Carolina offense, it wasn't necessarily smooth.

 Young had practices in which he looked like a bona fide star against his own defense. He also was stifled for prolonged stretches of joint practices against the Jaguars and Houston Texans .

 The starting offense's preseason performance will also do little to squash the outside concern for slow starts. Idzik and Young, though, feel comfortable with each other enough to make adjustments in the games that actually count.

 "I think it's been a really good learning period for us," Young said about training camp following the joint practice against the Jaguars.

 Backup quarterback Kenny Pickett , who signed with the team in March, has been in the room with Young and Idzik all summer. So has third-year quarterbacks coach Will Harriger. Both have seen Young and Idzik sort through the intricacies of each other's work.

 The comfort is there, and onlookers say it's evident.

 "I just think it's the natural evolution of an ever-deepening relationship," Herriger said. "And it's just nice that now, as the playcaller, [Idzik] has already got those two years of kind of developing a feel and kind of a general idea of what he thinks Bryce is going to say, but then ... he obviously makes a great attempt to get his opinion on that stuff as it goes."

 "You can tell it's [Young's] third year in the system," Pickett said. "I feel like he has a really good grasp of the offense. ... Has had these plays multiple times versus multiple different looks, so he knows where to go with the football with what he sees. He's playing really fast, so it's been really cool to work with him."

 

 
 THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN Idzik and Young has naturally evolved over the past three offseasons. But the 34-year-old coordinator has gone out of his way to build a bond with the signal-caller, too.

 Since his arrival in 2024, the coordinator and his wife, Emily, have hosted the quarterbacks at their home during offseason downtime.

 To Idzik, whose father, John Jr., was an NFL general manager, and grandfather, John Sr., was an NFL offensive coordinator, the ability to relate to his players on and off the field -- in particular, his quarterback -- is paramount.

 "Anytime you can welcome someone into your life and into your personal space, I think it's an important invitation of your intentions," Idzik said. "And him understanding I don't want to just go grab dinner at the fancy restaurant. I want you to come over to my house, so you understand who I am and what I care about. I want you to meet my wife and my dogs and see my living space so you have an idea of ... why I coach. This is my 'why.'"

 The message has been received by Young, who inherits his fourth playcaller in as many NFL seasons.

 "Just being able to meet the people in our lives, have that relationship [off the field], you want to go that much harder, do that much more for those people when you know the other side," Young said.

 That personal connection has bled into their shared work on 200 South Tryon Street. Young has trust in Idzik, and the coordinator wants the quarterback's continuous input, no matter how much it clashes with his point of view.

 

 It's a partnership, and Young and Idzik's careers will be intertwined based on how the offense performs this season. Finding a common ground is essential, not only for the two main stewards of the offense, but the unit and the team as well.

 "As a quarterback, you gotta get comfortable with the words yourself and where all the bones are buried on plays," Idzik said. "And then from there, he does a great job of recommending things that fit what we're trying to do as a whole."

 "We've been doing so much work behind the scenes," Young said. "So since Day 1, since right when he got hired and first gave me a call from that first conversation till now, it's been great being able to work with him. I feel like we have great chemistry and a great working relationship, so I'm excited for it to continue to grow."

 Canales, during his first season at the helm for the franchise, benched Young three weeks into the 2024 regular season.

 The then-second-year QB stood on the sideline with a clipboard for five games, as well-traveled veteran fill-in Andy Dalton led the Panthers to a 1-4 record. Young reemerged as the starter in Week 8 after his replacement sustained a thumb injury in a minor car accident.

 Canales has noted publicly that Young showed improved command of the offense during his first game back in the starting lineup against the Denver Broncos in a 28-14 road loss. Young has since thrown for 4,891 yards, 36 touchdowns and 15 interceptions, while leading the Panthers to a 2025 NFC South title -- albeit with an 8-9 overall record (Dalton started one loss due to…

title: Life without Myles Garrett: What to expect from Browns defense
summary: Cleveland still expects to field one of the NFL's stingiest defenses -- with a new coordinator, Jared Verse and plenty of returning talent.
full_text:
BEREA, Ohio -- Over the course of a few months, the Cleveland Browns lost two pillars of their elite defense.

 In February, Jim Schwartz, the architect of one of the league's best units over the past three seasons, resigned from his position as defensive coordinator after being passed over for the head coaching job that went to Todd Monken.

 Four months later, the Browns traded defensive end Myles Garrett , the two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and the league's single-season sack leader, to the Los Angeles Rams .

 

 Despite the departures, Cleveland still expects to field one of the stingiest defenses in the NFL -- with a new coordinator in Mike Rutenberg bringing fresh ideas, the 2024 NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year in Jared Verse arriving to lead the pass rush, and plenty of returning talent.

 "I see it as very similar to who we've been in the past," Monken said. "[Rutenberg will] put his own spin on it, and the staff as a collective whole. This is the Cleveland Browns' defense, just like it was last year.

 "Between our staff and 'Rudy' putting together the best plan, almost the same question: what do they believe in, and then what do our players do well? But I see a lot of similar things; we're going to be an attacking-style defense."

 
 Same front, a new leader 
 Well before the Browns entertained the idea of trading Garrett to the Rams, they hired Rutenberg, a former Atlanta Falcons assistant, to keep the foundation of their defense intact: a four-down-linemen scheme with an attacking front.

 Rutenberg, a first-time NFL coordinator, spent a large portion of his coaching career alongside Tennessee Titans coach Robert Saleh, who has used similar defensive fronts as Schwartz did. In 2025, Rutenberg worked with Falcons DC Jeff Ulbrich, another former Saleh assistant.

 Verse, a two-time Pro Bowler who arrived in Cleveland via the blockbuster Garrett trade, steps into the hole vacated by Garrett with his sights on improving from his 12-sack total over his first two seasons.

 Depth along the defensive line has been a concern for the Browns in training camp. Cleveland lost Alex Wright , who was projected to start at defensive end opposite Verse, to a ruptured Achilles two weeks ago . Even before Wright's injury, the Browns had scoured the edge rusher market for depth, hosting veterans Jadeveon Clowney and  Za'Darius Smith  before they signed elsewhere.

 The Browns, though, got much-needed reinforcements last week when linebacker Carson Schwesinger and defensive tackle Maliek Collins returned from injuries that sidelined them for the majority of training camp. Before Collins' season-ending quad injury last December, he was having his most productive season with 6.5 sacks. He returns to the middle of the defense alongside second-year player Mason Graham . The No. 5 overall pick in the 2025 draft, Graham recorded a half-sack as a rookie but was 20th in ESPN's pass rush win rate as an interior defender.

 

 It'll take a collective effort to make up for the NFL-record 23 sacks that Garrett produced last season, but the Browns are hoping it starts with Verse, who already has a reputation for being one of the best bull rushers in the NFL.

 Now the center of a new-look defensive line, Verse told ESPN he learned invaluable lessons from his time with a similarly formidable unit in Los Angeles.

 "The first thing I learned was you can trust your teammates," Verse told ESPN. "You don't got to make every superhero play. You don't got to be that superhero. But then the thing I also learned was to throw that out the window sometimes. Sometimes you have to put that cape back on. Sometimes you got to take those little glasses off and be Superman. You got to make those plays that it might not be your play, but you have to make it.

 "You can't always rely on your teammates, and your teammates can't always just rely on you because sometimes I'm going to mess up, they're going to mess up, and we're going to have to be able to clean each other up."

 
 Changes in the secondary 
 Where Rutenberg will leave his imprint most heavily is on the back end. Already one of the best man coverage secondaries, the Browns are aiming to confuse quarterbacks with increased pre- and post-snap disguises. In Atlanta, Rutenberg was the pass-game coordinator for a defense that was tied for sixth in the league with 16 interceptions last season (Cleveland was tied for 16th with 11).

 Where Garrett acknowledged that Schwartz was almost "stubborn" in his static approach, Rutenberg wants quarterbacks to hesitate by constantly changing what they see before and after the snap. Cleveland disguised its coverage on 19.8% of opponent dropbacks in 2025, which ranked 28th in the league. Atlanta disguised its coverage at a slightly higher rate, 22.9%, which ranked 20th during the same span.

 

 Maybe tellingly, the Browns' defense racked up nearly two dozen interceptions during training camp.

 "I think that this exotic defense that Rudy has, it's a lot of communication," safety Grant Delpit said. "It's a lot of disguise. It's a lot of confusion for the offense."

 And on a defense that already used three-safety lineups frequently, its usage could increase even more after drafting safety Emmanuel McNeil-Warren in the second round of the 2026 NFL draft. Coaches and teammates have raved about McNeil-Warren's athleticism at 6-3 and 210 pounds and the flexibility he could offer on the field -- in pass coverage and run defense.

 Still, Rutenberg doesn't want the essence of a defense that has allowed the fewest yards since 2023 to change. That means, even with the tweaks here and there, playing to his players' strengths, whether it be letting corners Denzel Ward and  Tyson Campbell  play sticky man coverage on an island, or allowing a physical and athletic front to be disruptive and penetrate into the backfield.

 "The key is players," Rutenberg said. "Players make every scheme, whether you're disguised or not, Cover 3, Cover 1, it doesn't matter; everybody runs similar skills. It's about getting guys to understand what we're trying to do, which they've done at the highest level, and giving players opportunities to be successful in whatever coverage or scheme we're in."

title: Jahdae Barron waiting his turn in loaded Broncos secondary
summary: Denver's secondary is stacked again, so Barron will once again face a battle to get on the field. But the 2025 first-round pick is set up for 2027 and beyond.
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- Jahdae Barron is clear on the math. Crystal clear.

 Despite being the Denver Broncos ' first-round draft pick in 2025 , the 24-year-old cornerback has been overshadowed -- in playing time, statistical production and in-game impact -- by players drafted before and after him. Such is life when one is dropped into what is arguably the NFL's best secondary.

 But Barron and the Broncos knew this would be the case when he was selected with the 20th overall pick last year. And his confidence regarding what he's capable of this season and beyond has not been dented.

 "You've got to be committed to the process without being emotionally attached to the results," Barron said. "At the end of the day, you wake up and you set goals every day, you just have to keep going ... you can't cheat the process."

 

 Barron's relative lack of playing time as a rookie isn't a deterrent, as he might have played more -- much more -- had he landed with any other NFL franchise. Browns linebacker Carson Schwesinger (No. 33 overall) was selected by a team that has won eight games the past two seasons. He played 956 snaps last season and won the league's Defensive Rookie of the Year award. Nick Emmanwori , picked by the Seahawks two spots after Schwesinger, slid into Seattle's open nickel spot immediately. But Barron joined a Broncos secondary that already had a ton of quality starters and now returns each of those players this season.

 Included are two players -- cornerback Pat Surtain II and safety Talanoa Hufanga  -- who earned second-team All-Pro honors last season. They are joined by fourth-year cornerback Riley Moss -- who Hufanga has called "one of the most athletic corners I've ever been around" -- safety Brandon Jones and nickel corner Ja'Quan McMillian , considered by many evaluators to be one of the best nickels in the league. Those five helped the Broncos' pass defense finish first in the NFL in yards allowed per dropback (4.95) and second in the NFL in both completion percentage allowed (57.8%) and yards allowed per pass attempt (6.1).

 "People have opinions and whatever the opinions, it truly doesn't matter," Barron said. "I'm going to wake up and eat the same exact food ... I'm going to text my mom. ... Nothing changes about my life ... I'm just going to continue meet my expectations and not somebody else's expectations."

 Those expectations could collide with increased playing time soon. Moss, McMillian and Jones are poised to be on a hearty list of Broncos scheduled to be unrestricted free agents next March. Moss and McMillian took similar paths to Barron, which the former first-rounder acknowledges.

 "As humans we want more, and we try and beat and rush the process," Barron said. "... You just have to stay true to what you believe in and sometimes it's hard. Sometimes you won't wake up in the mood, it won't be your day, but at the end of the day, you've got to be strong."

 He has a high bar to clear for more playing time in the short term. Surtain was voted as the best cornerback in the league in an ESPN poll of coaches, scouts and league personnel executives. Moss is the most challenged man-to-man cornerback in the league because of Surtain's presence and possesses the kind of athleticism and competitiveness the Broncos want opposite the All-Pro.

 But Barron is doing his part to make his case for more playing time in 2026 and down the road. He returned an interception 97 yards for a touchdown in the preseason opener against the Falcons. He is also one of the fastest players in the league (he ran a 4.39 40-yard dash at the 2025 combine at 194 pounds), and his positional versatility allows him to move around the defense.

 

 Barron is also known as a sure tackler, with several league personnel executives saying he didn't miss one in his final season at Texas. That gave the Broncos the liberty to play him at outside corner, nickel corner, safety and as a linebacker in the team's dime package (six defensive backs) last season, a menu that should be similar this year.

 "He wants more, obviously, I want more for him," Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph said. "... But I've said, we have a good secondary, and for us to have three or four or five good corners, that's a good thing, not a bad thing ... it's about finding those places where he can help us."

 That won't involve a position move, as Broncos coach Sean Payton has made it clear that cornerback will be Barron's primary job.

 "I read somewhere where we moved him to safety ... I'm not [moving him]," Payton said. "He's playing nickel, he's playing corner and then when we get into dime, he replaces a linebacker. So, he's doing really good."

 Assuming the Broncos stay healthy, 2026 might not see a big uptick of snaps for Barron. But he believes all the multitasking is good for the long game of his career.

 "Once you're at so many different positions, it allows you to understand everybody else's job ... and when you know everybody else's job, it allows you to know what kind of leverage you're supposed to be in," Barron said. "Right now it's still working parts, working movements, but I look down the line and it's going to be amazing."
